knowledge_statements.title: Affine-Slack Cone Form
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional primal conic program with an explicit affine slack.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(A:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) be linear, let \(b\in\mathbb{R}^m\), \(c\in\mathbb{R}^n\), and let \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^m\) be a nonempty closed convex cone. The affine-slack cone form is
\[\inf_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n,\,s\in K}\{\langle c,x\rangle:Ax+s=b\}.\]
Equivalently, eliminating the slack gives \(b-Ax\in K\). Thus a solver-facing primal point is the pair \((x,s)\), its affine residual is \(r_p=Ax+s-b\), and primal feasibility is exactly \(r_p=0\) together with \(s\in K\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A conic constraint is represented by an explicit cone slack satisfying an affine equation; feasibility requires zero affine residual and cone membership.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^m\) is a nonempty closed convex cone.
\(A:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) is linear.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Ax+s=b,\ s\in K\iff b-Ax\in K\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation is mathematically correct and fits the leaf, but the cited locator is specifically for second-order cone programs while the record asserts the form for an arbitrary nonempty closed convex cone. The flagged general-cone extension requires a directly supporting conic-optimization source.

knowledge_statements.title: Dual-Cone Adjoint Form
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lagrange dual associated with the affine-slack primal convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the primal problem \(\inf\{\langle c,x\rangle:Ax+s=b,\ s\in K\}\), define \(K^*=\{y:\langle y,s\rangle\ge 0\ \text{for every }s\in K\}\). Its dual-cone adjoint form is
\[\sup_{y\in K^*}\{-\langle b,y\rangle:A^*y+c=0\}.\]
For any primal-feasible \((x,s)\) and dual-feasible \(y\), the duality gap satisfies
\[\langle c,x\rangle+\langle b,y\rangle=\langle s,y\rangle\ge0.\]
Consequently, zero gap is equivalent to complementary orthogonality \(\langle s,y\rangle=0\) for feasible points.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The dual variable lies in the dual cone, satisfies the adjoint stationarity equation, and yields a nonnegative gap equal to slack–dual complementarity.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^m\) is a nonempty closed convex cone.
The primal convention is \(Ax+s=b\) with \(s\in K\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(y\in K^*,\ A^*y+c=0\Longrightarrow \langle c,x\rangle+\langle b,y\rangle=\langle s,y\rangle\ge0\).

notation.meaning: dual cone under the Euclidean pairing
adjoint of the primal affine operator

knowledge_statements.title: Heterogeneous Cone Blocks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Product-cone encoding whose component cones may have different types and dimensions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(K_i\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{m_i}\) be nonempty closed convex cones for \(i=1,\ldots,q\), and set \(K=K_1\times\cdots\times K_q\). Under the block decompositions \(s=(s_1,\ldots,s_q)\), \(b=(b_1,\ldots,b_q)\), and \(Ax=((A_1x),\ldots,(A_qx))\), the constraint
\[Ax+s=b,\qquad s\in K\]
is equivalent to \(A_ix+s_i=b_i\) and \(s_i\in K_i\) for every \(i\). Moreover, \(K^*=K_1^*\times\cdots\times K_q^*\), and Euclidean projection separates as \(\Pi_K(s)=(\Pi_{K_1}s_1,\ldots,\Pi_{K_q}s_q)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Different cone types and dimensions combine as a Cartesian product; membership, dual cones, affine residuals, and projections decompose blockwise.
assumptions_latex: Each \(K_i\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{m_i}\) is a nonempty closed convex cone.
The ambient product space carries the standard product inner product.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(s\in\prod_iK_i\iff (\forall i)\ s_i\in K_i\), with \((\prod_iK_i)^*=\prod_iK_i^*\).

notation.meaning: the cone assigned to block i
the row block of the affine operator for block i
Euclidean projection onto the product cone

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Cartesian-product cone membership, duality, and Euclidean projection are standard finite-dimensional convex-analysis identities
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Cartesian-product membership, dual-cone, and projection identities are standard and the representation fits the leaf, but no inspectable citation is supplied for the nontrivial duality and projection claims.

children.title: Repeated Cone Blocks
children.top_down_role: Cone programs containing multiple instances of a common block type.

knowledge_statements.title: Repeated Cone Blocks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A single cone type repeated within one product-cone instance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(K_0\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\) be a nonempty closed convex cone and let \(r\ge1\). A repeated-cone block is the product \(K_0^r\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{rd}\), represented by \(s=(s_1,\ldots,s_r)\). Then
\[s\in K_0^r\iff s_j\in K_0\quad(j=1,\ldots,r).\]
Its dual is \((K_0^*)^r\), and its projection is componentwise: \(\Pi_{K_0^r}(s)=(\Pi_{K_0}s_1,\ldots,\Pi_{K_0}s_r)\). A solver may therefore store one cone descriptor and the repetition count \(r\), provided block boundaries and ordering are fixed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: One cone descriptor can represent several equal-dimensional product factors, with membership, dualization, and projection performed independently on each repetition.
assumptions_latex: \(K_0\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\) is a nonempty closed convex cone.
\(r\) is a positive integer.

notation.meaning: r-fold Cartesian product of one cone

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: repeated cone blocks are finite Cartesian products of an identical closed convex cone
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The repeated-product identities are mathematically standard and the representation kind fits the leaf. A source is still required, particularly for the solver-facing claim that one descriptor plus a repetition count is a valid storage representation.

children.title: Batched Cone Blocks
children.top_down_role: Grouped processing of cone blocks across instances or workloads.

knowledge_statements.title: Batched Cone Blocks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Parallel storage of independent conic instances with a declared batch index.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For batch indices \(k=1,\ldots,B\), let \(K^{(k)}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{m_k}\) be nonempty closed convex cones and let \(A^{(k)}x^{(k)}+s^{(k)}=b^{(k)}\). The batched cone-block representation is the product feasibility system
\[s=(s^{(1)},\ldots,s^{(B)})\in\prod_{k=1}^B K^{(k)},\qquad A^{(k)}x^{(k)}+s^{(k)}=b^{(k)}\ \text{for every }k.\]
No constraint couples distinct batch indices. Hence cone projections and affine residuals may be evaluated independently, with \(r_p^{(k)}=A^{(k)}x^{(k)}+s^{(k)}-b^{(k)}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A batch groups independent conic systems under one outer index; each instance retains its own cone, data, projection, and residual.
assumptions_latex: \(B\) is a positive integer.
Each \(K^{(k)}\) is a nonempty closed convex cone.
There are no cross-batch constraints.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(s\in\prod_kK^{(k)}\iff (\forall k)\ s^{(k)}\in K^{(k)}\), and all residual evaluations separate by \(k\).

notation.meaning: primal affine residual of batch member k

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: an uncoupled batch is a Cartesian product of independent finite-dimensional conic systems
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The uncoupled product interpretation is plausible and locally appropriate, but no source is supplied for the batching convention. The domains of each A^{(k)} and x^{(k)} are also not explicitly introduced, so a sourced mathematical specification is needed.

children.title: Repeated-Block Batch Layouts
children.top_down_role: Data layouts that expose repeated cone structure to batched solver operations.

knowledge_statements.title: Repeated-Block Batch Layouts
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tensorized layout combining an outer batch with repeated inner cone factors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let every batch member contain \(r\) factors of a cone \(K_0\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\). Store the slacks as an array \(S=(s_{k,j})\in\mathbb{R}^{B\times r\times d}\), where \(k\) is the batch index and \(j\) is the repeated-block index. With a fixed vectorization order,
\[\operatorname{vec}(S)\in K_0^{Br}\iff s_{k,j}\in K_0\quad\text{for all }k=1,\ldots,B,\ j=1,\ldots,r.\]
Projection and dual-cone membership act independently on the \(Br\) slices. Any permutation of slices represents the same abstract product cone if the affine data and diagnostic outputs use the identical permutation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A batch of repeated blocks is a three-axis array whose cone operations separate over every batch-and-repetition slice; ordering must remain consistent.
assumptions_latex: \(K_0\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\) is a nonempty closed convex cone.
\(B,r\) are positive integers.
A vectorization order is fixed consistently across all solver data.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{vec}(S)\in K_0^{Br}\iff (\forall k,j)\ s_{k,j}\in K_0\).

notation.meaning: repetition index within a batch member

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The product-cone membership identity is correct for a consistent vectorization, and the representation kind matches the layout leaf. The tensor layout and permutation-consistency claims nevertheless lack an inspectable solver or mathematical source.

knowledge_statements.title: Primal–Dual Saddle Form
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex–concave saddle representation of the affine-slack conic program.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^m\) be a nonempty closed convex cone. The primal problem \(\inf_x\{\langle c,x\rangle:b-Ax\in K\}\) has the saddle representation
\[\inf_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n}\sup_{y\in K^*}\mathcal{L}(x,y),\qquad \mathcal{L}(x,y)=\langle c,x\rangle+\langle y,Ax-b\rangle.\]
Indeed, the supremum over \(K^*\) is zero when \(b-Ax\in K\) and is \(+\infty\) otherwise. A saddle point \((x^*,y^*)\) satisfies primal feasibility, \(A^*y^*+c=0\), and \(\langle y^*,b-Ax^*\rangle=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The conic program is a convex–concave minimax problem whose saddle conditions are primal feasibility, adjoint stationarity, and complementarity.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^m\) is a nonempty closed convex cone.
\(A:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) is linear.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\inf_x\{\langle c,x\rangle:b-Ax\in K\}=\inf_x\sup_{y\in K^*}\mathcal{L}(x,y)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Monotone-Inclusion Form
knowledge_statements.scope_note: KKT system represented as a zero of a set-valued monotone operator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
On \(\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}^m\), define
\[\mathcal{M}(x,y)=\begin{pmatrix}c+A^*y\\ b-Ax+N_{K^*}(y)\end{pmatrix},\]
where \(N_{K^*}\) is the convex-analytic normal cone. Then the primal–dual optimality system for the saddle function \(\mathcal{L}(x,y)=\langle c,x\rangle+\langle y,Ax-b\rangle-\delta_{K^*}(y)\) is
\[0\in\mathcal{M}(x,y).\]
The skew linear coupling \((x,y)\mapsto(A^*y,-Ax)\), the constant vector \((c,b)\), and the normal-cone operator together make \(\mathcal{M}\) monotone; in finite dimensions it is maximally monotone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The conic KKT conditions are the zeros of a maximally monotone operator combining adjoint coupling, affine data, and a dual-cone normal cone.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^m\) is a nonempty closed convex cone.
All spaces are finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((x,y)\) satisfies the primal–dual KKT system if and only if \(0\in\mathcal{M}(x,y)\).

notation.meaning: normal-cone operator of the dual cone
indicator function of the dual cone

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: convex KKT systems are standard zeros of a skew linear map plus a normal-cone operator
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed inclusion has the correct signs for the stated saddle function, and maximal monotonicity is valid in the declared finite-dimensional setting. However, the KKT equivalence and maximal-monotonicity assertion are nontrivial and have no cited source.

children.title: Resolvent Form
children.top_down_role: Conic splitting representations centered on resolvent operators.

knowledge_statements.title: Resolvent Form
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Resolvent of a set-valued operator on a finite-dimensional Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H\) be a finite-dimensional real Hilbert space, let \(M:H\rightrightarrows H\), and let \(\gamma>0\). The resolvent of \(\gamma M\) is
\[J_{\gamma M}=(I+\gamma M)^{-1}.\]
Thus \(u=J_{\gamma M}(z)\) exactly when
\[z\in u+\gamma M(u),\qquad\text{equivalently}\qquad \frac{z-u}{\gamma}\in M(u).\]
If \(M\) is maximally monotone, \(J_{\gamma M}\) is everywhere defined, single-valued, and firmly nonexpansive. Moreover, \(0\in M(u)\) if and only if \(u=J_{\gamma M}(u)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A resolvent solves an implicit operator step; zeros of the operator are precisely fixed points of its resolvent.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a finite-dimensional real Hilbert space.
\(M:H\rightrightarrows H\) is maximally monotone when global single-valuedness is asserted.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(u=J_{\gamma M}(z)\iff (z-u)/\gamma\in M(u)\), and \(0\in M(u)\iff J_{\gamma M}(u)=u\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: resolvent definition and firm nonexpansiveness are standard maximal-monotone operator theory
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The resolvent definition and fixed-point characterization are correct, and maximal monotonicity supplies the stated global single-valued firmly nonexpansive mapping. These nontrivial operator-theory properties require an inspectable citation.

children.title: Reflected-Resolvent Form
children.top_down_role: Conic splitting representations centered on reflected-resolvent operators.

knowledge_statements.title: Reflected-Resolvent Form
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reflection generated by a resolvent of a monotone operator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H\) be a finite-dimensional real Hilbert space, let \(M:H\rightrightarrows H\), and let \(\gamma>0\). The reflected resolvent of \(\gamma M\) is
\[R_{\gamma M}=2J_{\gamma M}-I,\qquad J_{\gamma M}=(I+\gamma M)^{-1}.\]
Equivalently, if \(u=J_{\gamma M}(z)\), then \(R_{\gamma M}(z)=2u-z\). If \(M\) is maximally monotone, the firm nonexpansiveness of \(J_{\gamma M}\) implies that \(R_{\gamma M}\) is nonexpansive. The fixed-point sets agree: \(\operatorname{Fix}(R_{\gamma M})=\operatorname{Fix}(J_{\gamma M})=\operatorname{zer}(M)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The reflected resolvent doubles a resolvent step and subtracts the input; for maximal monotone operators it is nonexpansive with the same fixed points.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a finite-dimensional real Hilbert space.
\(M:H\rightrightarrows H\) is maximally monotone when nonexpansiveness is asserted.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R_{\gamma M}=2J_{\gamma M}-I\) and \(\operatorname{Fix}(R_{\gamma M})=\operatorname{zer}(M)\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: the reflected-resolvent identity and nonexpansiveness correspondence are standard operator theory
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition, nonexpansiveness implication, and fixed-point-set identity are correct for the stated setting, and definition is an appropriate kind for this leaf. No source is supplied for the operator-theory properties.

children.title: Resolvent–Reflection Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Structural correspondence between resolvent-based and reflection-based representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Resolvent–Reflection Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Invertible affine correspondence between resolvent and reflected-resolvent operators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For any operator \(M:H\rightrightarrows H\) and \(\gamma>0\) for which the resolvent is single-valued, the resolvent and reflected resolvent determine one another by
\[R_{\gamma M}=2J_{\gamma M}-I,
\qquad
J_{\gamma M}=\frac{I+R_{\gamma M}}{2}.\]
Consequently, \(J_{\gamma M}\) is firmly nonexpansive if and only if \(R_{\gamma M}\) is nonexpansive. Their residuals differ only by scale:
\[I-R_{\gamma M}=2(I-J_{\gamma M}).\]
They therefore have the same fixed-point set, which equals \(\operatorname{zer}(M)\) when \(J_{\gamma M}=(I+\gamma M)^{-1}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Resolvents and reflected resolvents are affine transforms of each other; firm nonexpansiveness becomes nonexpansiveness, and their residuals differ by a factor of two.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a finite-dimensional real Hilbert space.
\(J_{\gamma M}\) is single-valued.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R_{\gamma M}=2J_{\gamma M}-I\iff J_{\gamma M}=(I+R_{\gamma M})/2\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: the correspondence follows from the defining affine relation between the two operators
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The affine correspondence and residual scaling are correct, but the statement begins with an operator on H without introducing H there, and the firm-nonexpansive/nonexpansive equivalence is uncited. A sourced version should explicitly declare the Hilbert space and the mapping domain.

knowledge_statements.title: Fixed-Point Residual-Map Form
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Diagnostic representation of an operator equation by a fixed-point residual.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(T:H\to H\) be a single-valued mapping on a finite-dimensional real Hilbert space. Define its fixed-point residual map by
\[F_T(z)=z-Tz.\]
Then the fixed-point problem \(z=Tz\) is exactly the root problem \(F_T(z)=0\), so \(\|F_T(z)\|\) is a directly computable absolute residual. For a scale \(d(z)>0\), a relative diagnostic may be reported as \(\|F_T(z)\|/d(z)\). If \(T=J_{\gamma M}\), then \(F_T(z)=z-u\) with \((z-u)/\gamma\in M(u)\), where \(u=Tz\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Subtracting an iteration map from the identity converts fixed points into residual zeros and supplies an absolute or scaled stopping diagnostic.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a finite-dimensional real Hilbert space.
\(T:H\to H\) is single-valued.
A relative residual uses a strictly positive declared scale \(d(z)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(z\in\operatorname{Fix}(T)\iff F_T(z)=0\), where \(F_T=I-T\).

notation.meaning: positive normalization scale for a relative residual

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: fixed points are exactly zeros of the identity-minus-operator residual
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The identity-minus-map representation and resolvent relation are correct and fit the diagnostic leaf. No citation supports the representation, and the relative residual scale d(z) is left arbitrary, so the record does not define a specific relative diagnostic beyond requiring positivity.

knowledge_statements.title: Subspace–Cone Intersection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasibility representation underlying homogeneous conic embeddings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(E\) be a finite-dimensional inner-product space, let \(C\subseteq E\) be a closed convex cone, and let \(L\subseteq E\) be a linear subspace. The homogeneous conic feasibility problem is
\[
\text{find }z\in L\cap C\setminus\{0\}.
\]
Equivalently, if \(L=\ker M\) for a linear map \(M:E\to F\), it is \(Mz=0\), \(z\in C\), \(z\ne0\). Because feasibility is scale invariant, a bounded normalization such as \(\langle e,z\rangle=1\), with \(e\in\operatorname{int}C^*\), may replace \(z\ne0\) whenever every desired ray has positive pairing with \(e\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A homogeneous conic problem seeks a nonzero point where a linear subspace intersects a closed convex cone, optionally using a scale-fixing normalization.
assumptions_latex: \(E\) is finite-dimensional.
\(C\subseteq E\) is a closed convex cone.
\(L\subseteq E\) is a linear subspace.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L\cap C\setminus\{0\}\) is the feasible set of nontrivial homogeneous solutions.

assumptions_latex: \(U\) is a finite-dimensional inner-product space.
\(C\subseteq U\) is a closed convex cone.
\(Q:U\to U\) is linear and satisfies \(Q^*=-Q\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((u,v)\in\operatorname{gra}Q\cap(C\times C^*)\) implies \(\langle u,v\rangle=0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operator graph form used by splitting-based conic solvers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(U\) be a finite-dimensional inner-product space, let \(C\subseteq U\) be a closed convex cone, and let \(Q:U\to U\) be skew-adjoint. Graph-form conic feasibility seeks \(u,v\in U\) satisfying
\[
v=Qu,\qquad u\in C,\qquad v\in C^*,\qquad (u,v)\ne(0,0).
\]
Equivalently,
\[
(u,v)\in\operatorname{gra}Q\cap(C\times C^*),\qquad (u,v)\ne(0,0).
\]
Skew-adjointness ensures \(\langle u,v\rangle=\langle u,Qu\rangle=0\), so every feasible pair is complementary. A normalization may be imposed to select one representative of each positive ray.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Graph form intersects the graph of a skew-adjoint operator with a primal-dual cone product; every nonzero feasible pair is complementary.

knowledge_statements.title: Solution-Recovery Outcomes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recovery rule for a homogeneous self-dual embedding.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider a homogeneous self-dual embedding whose variables include primal-dual components \((x,y,s)\) and nonnegative scalars \((\tau,\kappa)\), with embedding equations chosen for a specified primal-dual conic pair. If an exact embedding solution satisfies \(\tau>0\) and \(\kappa=0\), then
\[
(\widehat x,\widehat y,\widehat s)=(x/\tau,y/\tau,s/\tau)
\]
satisfies the original primal and dual feasibility equations and has zero duality gap. Thus this branch certifies simultaneous primal-dual optimality; numerical recovery additionally requires residuals and cone violations after scaling to lie within the declared tolerances.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive homogenizing scalar permits division by that scalar, recovering primal-dual feasible variables with zero gap in the exact embedding.
assumptions_latex: The embedding correctly represents a specified primal-dual conic pair.
The embedding solution is exact.
\(\tau>0\) and \(\kappa=0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((x/\tau,y/\tau,s/\tau)\) is a primal-dual optimal solution.

source_refs.source_title: Semidefinite Optimization and Convex Algebraic Geometry

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\) and \(E\) be finite-dimensional inner-product spaces, let \(K\subseteq E\) be a closed convex cone, let \(A:X\to E\) be linear, and let \(b\in E\). For the feasibility system
\[
Ax+s=b,\qquad x\in X,\qquad s\in K,
\]
a vector \(y\in E\) is a strong infeasibility certificate if
\[
A^*y=0,\qquad y\in K^*,\qquad \langle b,y\rangle<0.
\]
The existence of such a vector certifies that the feasibility system is empty. In a homogeneous embedding, an outcome with \(\tau=0\) is classified as primal infeasibility only when a recovered nonzero ray can be normalized and satisfies these adjoint, cone-membership, and strict-separation conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Primal infeasibility is certified by a dual-cone vector that annihilates the linear image and strictly separates the right-hand side.

children.title: Unboundedness Outcomes
children.top_down_role: Embedding outcomes supporting primal or dual unboundedness interpretation.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are finite-dimensional inner-product spaces.
\(K\subseteq X\) is a closed convex cone, \(A:X\to Y\) is linear, \(b\in Y\), and \(c\in X\).
There exist \(x_0,d\in X\) such that \(x_0\in K\), \(Ax_0=b\), \(d\in K\), \(Ad=0\), and \(\langle c,d\rangle<0\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primal improving-ray outcome for a standard conic program.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be finite-dimensional inner-product spaces, let \(K\subseteq X\) be a closed convex cone, let \(A:X\to Y\) be linear, and let \(b\in Y\) and \(c\in X\). Consider
\[
\inf\{\langle c,x\rangle:Ax=b,\ x\in K\}.
\]
A direction \(d\in X\) certifies primal unboundedness when there exists a feasible point \(x_0\in K\) such that
\[
Ax_0=b,\qquad d\in K,\qquad Ad=0,\qquad \langle c,d\rangle<0.
\]
Under these conditions, the objective infimum is \(-\infty\). An embedding ray is assigned this outcome only after the improving-direction conditions and the existence of a feasible base point are verified.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible conic program is unbounded below when it has a cone direction that preserves the equations and strictly decreases the objective.
knowledge_statements.title: Unboundedness Outcomes

children.title: Infeasibility–Unboundedness Ambiguity
children.top_down_role: Numerical regimes where the two outcome classes are difficult to distinguish.

knowledge_statements.title: Infeasibility–Unboundedness Ambiguity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between alternative certificates and definitive solver status.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A homogeneous embedding vector with \(\tau=0\) does not by itself distinguish infeasibility from unboundedness. Classification requires a nonzero recovered component satisfying either a strict separating-certificate inequality or a strict improving-ray inequality. If all candidate strict margins vanish, or their signs are unresolved within tolerance, then the embedding supplies no definitive alternative certificate. Moreover, an improving ray without an independently verified feasible point does not alone prove unboundedness; it may coexist with primal infeasibility. The mathematically valid output is therefore an ambiguous or indeterminate status rather than either definitive label.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Zero homogenization alone is inconclusive; a verified strict certificate margin, and sometimes a feasible base point, is required to distinguish outcomes.
assumptions_latex: The embedding solution satisfies \(\tau=0\).
No candidate certificate has a verified strict margin.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Neither infeasibility nor unboundedness is certified by the embedding vector alone.

knowledge_statements.title: Facial-Reduction Outcomes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reduction to the minimal cone face containing feasible slacks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(Ax+s=b\), \(s\in K\), initialize \(F_0=K\). At iteration \(i\), find an exposing vector \(y_i\in F_i^*\) satisfying
\[
A^*y_i=0,
\qquad \langle b,y_i\rangle=0,
\qquad F_i\not\subseteq y_i^\perp,
\]
and set \(F_{i+1}=F_i\cap y_i^\perp\). Stop when no such reducing certificate exists or when the reduced system has a slack in \(\operatorname{ri}F_i\). The output is the reduced cone face together with the exposing sequence; if the process reaches a face disjoint from the affine slack space, the sequence supports an infeasibility outcome.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Facial reduction repeatedly intersects the cone with exposed faces until relative strict feasibility is obtained or infeasibility is exposed.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a closed convex cone.
Each selected \(y_i\) satisfies the displayed reduction conditions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output face contains every feasible slack and is strictly smaller at each successful reduction.

children.title: Degenerate Embedding Outcomes
children.top_down_role: Embedding outcomes affected by degeneracy in recovered solution or certificate information.

knowledge_statements.title: Degenerate Embedding Outcomes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact zero-scalar branch lacking a recoverable strict certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let an exact homogeneous self-dual embedding solution have nonnegative scalars \((\tau,\kappa)\). The branch
\[
\tau=0,
\qquad \kappa=0
\]
is degenerate: division by \(\tau\) cannot recover a primal-dual solution, while \(\kappa\) supplies no positive normalization for an alternative certificate. Unless another nonzero component independently satisfies a complete infeasibility or improving-ray certificate with a strict margin, the embedding point certifies no original-problem status. The zero embedding point is the canonical example and must be excluded by normalization or a nontriviality test.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When both embedding scalars vanish, neither solution recovery nor certificate normalization is available without an independently verifiable nonzero ray.
assumptions_latex: The embedding solution is exact.
\(\tau=\kappa=0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: No definitive original-problem outcome follows without an additional strict certificate.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind fits, but the interpretation of the simultaneous zero-scalar branch depends materially on the exact homogeneous self-dual embedding equations and normalization identities. The generic self-dual-embedding locator has not been inspected closely enough to establish that kappa always has the asserted certificate-normalization role or that the stated exception is exhaustive.

children.title: Indeterminate Embedding Outcomes
children.top_down_role: Embedding outcomes lacking reliable classification as solution or certificate states.

knowledge_statements.title: Indeterminate Embedding Outcomes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tolerance-level boundary for solver-facing outcome classification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(r_{m emb}\) denote the embedding residual, and let \(m_{m sol}\), \(m_{m inf}\), and \(m_{m ray}\) denote respectively the recovery, separating-certificate, and improving-ray margins after normalization. Given declared tolerances, an outcome is indeterminate whenever \(r_{m emb}\) is unacceptable or none of the mutually interpreted tests has a verified margin: positive recoverable \(\tau\), strict infeasibility separation, or strict objective improvement. In particular, quantities numerically compatible with \(\tau=0\), \(\kappa=0\), and zero certificate margins cannot support a definitive label, even if the iterate nearly satisfies the embedding equations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An approximate embedding outcome is indeterminate when residuals are excessive or every recovery and certificate margin is unresolved at the chosen tolerances.
assumptions_latex: All residuals and margins use fixed scaling and declared tolerances.
No outcome test has a verified strict margin.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The solver must return an indeterminate status rather than a definitive solution or certificate status.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind matches the leaf, but the claimed status rule depends on solver-specific residual definitions, scaling, normalization, and tolerance semantics. With no citation, the meanings of the margins and the mandatory indeterminate classification cannot be validated.

children.title: Outcome Disambiguation Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Numerical boundaries separating degenerate evidence from indeterminate evidence.

knowledge_statements.title: Outcome Disambiguation Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Decision conditions separating solution, certificate, and unresolved branches.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix scale-aware tolerances \(\epsilon_{m emb},\epsilon_{\rm cone},\epsilon_{m gap}>0\). A definitive outcome requires: embedding residual at most \(\epsilon_{m emb}\); cone-distance violations at most \(\epsilon_{m cone}\); and exactly one applicable recovery test with a margin exceeding \(\epsilon_{m gap}\). A solution outcome additionally requires safely positive \(\tau\) and acceptable rescaled primal, dual, and gap residuals. An infeasibility or unboundedness outcome requires its complete normalized ray certificate and strict signed margin. If tests overlap, depend on an unsafe division, or remain within their tolerance boundary, the outcome is indeterminate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Definitive classification requires acceptable residuals and one complete test with a margin safely beyond tolerance; boundary or overlapping tests remain indeterminate.
assumptions_latex: Tolerances are fixed before classification.
Residuals are evaluated under a common scaling convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Only a uniquely validated test outside its tolerance boundary receives a definitive status.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition kind is appropriate, but the universal requirement that exactly one test apply is not a standard embedding-independent condition and may fail for implementations whose valid certificates overlap. The numerical policy also depends on unspecified scaling and residual definitions. An authoritative solver or embedding specification is required.

knowledge_statements.title: Extended-Dual Embeddings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lifted dual representation designed to restore exact conic alternatives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(K\subseteq E\) be a closed convex cone and let \(F\unlhd K\) be a face containing every feasible slack of a conic system. An extended-dual embedding replaces a possibly unattained certificate in \(K^*\) by lifted variables \(w\) in a product cone \(\mathcal K_{m ext}\) and a linear map \(T\) satisfying
\[
T(\mathcal K_{m ext})=F^*.
\]
The embedded dual feasibility conditions are imposed on \(w\), while the original dual object is recovered as \(T w\). When the chosen lift represents \(F^*\) exactly, certificates unavailable in the unreduced dual can be represented in the extension.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An extended dual lifts the dual of the minimal feasible face, allowing exact representation of certificates that the unreduced dual may not attain.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is a face of the closed convex cone \(K\).
The lift satisfies \(T(\mathcal K_{m ext})=F^*\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every element of \(F^*\) has a lifted conic representation \(T w\) with \(w\in\mathcal K_{m ext}\).

notation.meaning: F is a face of K

knowledge_statements.title: Projective Homogenization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Embedding affine conic feasibility into homogeneous projective coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\subseteq E\) be a cone and consider the affine conic system \(Az=b\), \(z\in C\). Its projective homogenization introduces \(\tau\ge0\) and forms
\[
Az=b\tau,
\qquad z\in C,
\qquad (z,	au)
e(0,0).
\]
Every affine feasible point \(\widehat z\) determines the projective ray \(\{(t\widehat z,t):t>0\}\). Conversely, every homogeneous feasible pair with \(\tau>0\) recovers the affine point \(\widehat z=z/\tau\). Feasible pairs with \(\tau=0\) satisfy \(Az=0\) and represent directions at infinity rather than finite affine points.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projective homogenization adds a scale coordinate: positive scale recovers affine solutions, while zero scale represents feasible directions at infinity.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a cone.
\(A:E\to F\) is linear.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\tau>0\) gives \(A(z/\tau)=b\), while \(\tau=0\) gives \(Az=0\).

knowledge_statements.title: Subspace–Cone Douglas–Rachford Splitting
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Douglas–Rachford iteration for feasibility between a linear subspace and a closed convex cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a linear subspace, let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a nonempty closed convex cone, and choose \(z^0\in\mathbb R^n\). For \(k=0,1,\ldots\), compute \(x^k=P_Sz^k\), \(y^k=P_C(2x^k-z^k)\), and \(z^{k+1}=z^k+y^k-x^k\). Equivalently, \(z^{k+1}=Tz^k\), where \(T=\tfrac12(I+R_CR_S)\) and \(R_D=2P_D-I\). Stop when \(\|x^k-y^k\|\) meets the prescribed feasibility tolerance; return \(x^k\) as the primal shadow and \(z^k-x^k\) as the associated normal component.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Alternate reflected projections onto the embedding subspace and cone; the shadow iterate supplies the feasible candidate and the projection gap supplies a residual.
assumptions_latex: \(S\) is a linear subspace of \(\mathbb R^n\).
\(C\) is a nonempty closed convex cone.
Euclidean projections onto \(S\) and \(C\) are computable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(z^{k+1}=\tfrac12(I+R_CR_S)z^k\), with diagnostic residual \(r^k=x^k-y^k\).

notation.meaning: Euclidean projection onto a closed convex set D

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits the leaf, and the displayed iteration is recognizable as subspace–cone Douglas–Rachford splitting. However, no cited evidence supports the iteration, stopping rule, primal-shadow interpretation, or claimed normal component. The plain statement also calls the process alternating reflected projections although the displayed method uses projected shadows and a Douglas–Rachford update.

knowledge_statements.title: Relaxed Douglas–Rachford Splitting
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constant-relaxation Douglas–Rachford method for subspace–cone feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S,C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) satisfy the stated projection assumptions, choose \(z^0\in\mathbb R^n\), and fix \(\lambda\in(0,2)\). At iteration \(k\), set \(x^k=P_Sz^k\), \(y^k=P_C(2x^k-z^k)\), and \(z^{k+1}=z^k+\lambda(y^k-x^k)\). Thus \(z^{k+1}=[(1-\lambda)I+\lambda T]z^k\), where \(T=\tfrac12(I+R_CR_S)\). Terminate when \(\|x^k-y^k\|\) is below tolerance and return the shadow \(x^k\). The choice \(\lambda=1\) recovers the unrelaxed iteration.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Scale the ordinary Douglas–Rachford displacement by a relaxation factor strictly between zero and two; factor one gives the basic method.
assumptions_latex: \(S\) is a linear subspace and \(C\) is a nonempty closed convex cone.
\(P_S\) and \(P_C\) are Euclidean projections.
The constant relaxation satisfies \(0<\lambda<2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(z^{k+1}=z^k+\lambda\bigl(P_C(2P_Sz^k-z^k)-P_Sz^k\bigr)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits the relaxed-splitting leaf, but no source is supplied. The admissible interval and the identification of lambda=1 as the unrelaxed method depend on the stated relaxation convention and require an authoritative algorithm locator.

knowledge_statements.title: Variable-Metric Douglas–Rachford Splitting
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Douglas–Rachford feasibility splitting in a fixed positive-definite metric.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\in\mathbb S_{++}^n\), define \(\|u\|_M^2=u^\top Mu\), and let \(P_D^M(z)=\mathop{\rm argmin}_{w\in D}\tfrac12\|w-z\|_M^2\). Starting from \(z^0\in\mathbb R^n\), compute \(x^k=P_S^Mz^k\), \(y^k=P_C^M(2x^k-z^k)\), and \(z^{k+1}=z^k+y^k-x^k\). Stop when \(\|x^k-y^k\|_M\) is within tolerance and return \(x^k\). This is ordinary Douglas–Rachford splitting in the Hilbert space whose inner product is \(\langle u,v\rangle_M=u^\top Mv\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Replace Euclidean projections and residual norms by projections and norms induced by one positive-definite metric.
assumptions_latex: \(M\in\mathbb S_{++}^n\) is fixed throughout the iteration.
\(S\) is a linear subspace and \(C\) is a nonempty closed convex cone.
The metric projections \(P_S^M\) and \(P_C^M\) are computable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(z^{k+1}=z^k+P_C^M(2P_S^Mz^k-z^k)-P_S^Mz^k\).

notation.meaning: projection onto D in the M-metric

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits the leaf and the fixed positive-definite-metric formulation is internally coherent. No evidence supports this particular variable-metric variant, its stopping diagnostic, or the shadow returned in the homogeneous-embedding context.

knowledge_statements.title: Two-Block Embedding ADMM
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scaled two-block ADMM applied to a subspace–cone feasibility formulation of a homogeneous embedding.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Represent the homogeneous embedding as \(\min_{u,v}\delta_S(u)+\delta_C(v)\) subject to \(u-v=0\), where \(S\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is the embedding subspace and \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is its product cone. Given \(v^0,d^0\in\mathbb R^n\) and \(\rho>0\), iterate \(u^{k+1}=P_S(v^k-d^k)\), \(v^{k+1}=P_C(u^{k+1}+d^k)\), and \(d^{k+1}=d^k+u^{k+1}-v^{k+1}\). Stop when both \(\|u^{k+1}-v^{k+1}\|\) and \(\rho\|v^{k+1}-v^k\|\) meet their tolerances; return the embedding variables decoded from \(v^{k+1}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Split the homogeneous embedding into subspace and cone blocks, project each block, and update the scaled consensus multiplier.
assumptions_latex: \(S\) is a linear subspace and \(C\) is a nonempty closed convex cone.
The embedding feasibility problem is equivalent to finding \(u=v\in S\cap C\).
The penalty parameter satisfies \(\rho>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(r^{k+1}=u^{k+1}-v^{k+1}\) and \(s^{k+1}=\rho(v^{k+1}-v^k)\) are the ADMM primal and dual diagnostics.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits the leaf, but the record has no citation for the asserted reduction of the homogeneous embedding to S-cap-C consensus, the scaled-multiplier sign convention, the residual definitions, or decoding of embedding variables. These choices are formulation-dependent.

knowledge_statements.title: Decomposed-SDP Embedding ADMM
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Consensus ADMM for a homogeneous SDP embedding represented by smaller positive-semidefinite blocks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X=(X_1,\ldots,X_p)\) with \(X_i\in\mathbb S^{n_i}\), let \(C=\prod_{i=1}^p\mathbb S_+^{n_i}\), and let \(S\) be the linear subspace imposing the homogeneous embedding equations and equality of all duplicated overlap entries. Starting with \(V^0,D^0\), perform \(U^{k+1}=P_S(V^k-D^k)\), \(V_i^{k+1}=P_{\mathbb S_+^{n_i}}(U_i^{k+1}+D_i^k)\) in parallel, and \(D^{k+1}=D^k+U^{k+1}-V^{k+1}\). Stop when the consensus residual and successive-block residual satisfy tolerance; reconstruct the global SDP matrix from the consistent blocks.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Apply consensus ADMM to duplicated SDP blocks: enforce embedding and overlap equations globally, then project each block independently onto its PSD cone.
assumptions_latex: The SDP decomposition is exact when overlap-consistency equations are imposed.
Each local cone is \(\mathbb S_+^{n_i}\).
The projection onto the embedding-consensus subspace is computable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(V_i^{k+1}=Q_i\max(\Lambda_i,0)Q_i^\top\) whenever \(U_i^{k+1}+D_i^k=Q_i\Lambda_iQ_i^\top\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits the decomposed-SDP ADMM leaf, but no source states the structural conditions under which duplicated PSD blocks plus overlap equalities exactly represent the global SDP. The embedding subspace, residual, reconstruction rule, and decomposition assumptions remain too source-dependent to validate.

children.title: Primal–Dual Hybrid Gradient for Cone Programs

knowledge_statements.title: Basic Conic PDHG
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Euclidean PDHG for a finite-dimensional conic program in equality form.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\min_{x\in K}c^\top x\) subject to \(Ax=b\), use the saddle function \(L(x,y)=c^\top x+\delta_K(x)+\langle Ax-b,y\rangle\). Choose \(x^0,y^0\), set \(\bar x^0=x^0\), and select \(\tau,\sigma>0\) with \(\tau\sigma\|A\|_2^2<1\). Iterate \(y^{k+1}=y^k+\sigma(A\bar x^k-b)\), \(x^{k+1}=P_K(x^k-\tau(c+A^\top y^{k+1}))\), and \(\bar x^{k+1}=x^{k+1}+\theta(x^{k+1}-x^k)\), where \(\theta\in[0,1]\). Stop using prescribed primal, dual, and gap residual tolerances; return \((x^{k+1},y^{k+1})\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Alternate a dual equality-residual step with a projected primal cone step, optionally extrapolating the new primal iterate.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is a nonempty closed convex cone.
\(A:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) is linear.
\(\tau\sigma\|A\|_2^2<1\) and \(0\leq\theta\leq1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(y^{k+1}=y^k+\sigma(A\bar x^k-b)\) and \(x^{k+1}=P_K(x^k-\tau(c+A^\top y^{k+1}))\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits Basic Conic PDHG, and the finite-dimensional updates are mathematically recognizable. No source supports the precise update ordering, extrapolation range, strict step-size condition, or the unspecified primal, dual, and gap diagnostics.

knowledge_statements.title: Scalar Primal–Dual Scaling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar step-size condition for Euclidean conic PDHG.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) be the coupling operator in conic PDHG. Scalar primal–dual scaling chooses constants \(\tau>0\) and \(\sigma>0\) and uses the primal metric \(T=\tau I_n\) and dual metric \(\Sigma=\sigma I_m\). A sufficient strict stability condition is \(\|\Sigma^{1/2}AT^{1/2}\|_2<1\), equivalently \(\tau\sigma\|A\|_2^2<1\). Writing \(\tau=\gamma/\widehat L\) and \(\sigma=1/(\gamma\widehat L)\), with \(\gamma>0\) and \(\widehat L>\|A\|_2\), preserves the product condition while changing the relative primal–dual scaling.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose positive scalar primal and dual steps whose product is below the reciprocal squared operator norm; their ratio controls primal–dual balance.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) is a finite-dimensional linear operator.
\(\tau>0\) and \(\sigma>0\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition kind is acceptable for this scaling leaf, and the scalar norm condition and parameterization are internally consistent. An authoritative source with a specific locator is nevertheless required for the claimed PDHG stability condition and scaling interpretation.

knowledge_statements.title: Diagonal Primal–Dual Preconditioning
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Diagonal metric selection and stability condition for preconditioned conic PDHG.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T=\operatorname{diag}(t_1,\ldots,t_n)\succ0\) and \(\Sigma=\operatorname{diag}(s_1,\ldots,s_m)\succ0\). Preconditioned PDHG replaces scalar steps by \(x^{k+1}=\operatorname{prox}_{f}^{T^{-1}}(x^k-TA^\top y^{k+1})\) and \(y^{k+1}=\operatorname{prox}_{g^*}^{\Sigma^{-1}}(y^k+\Sigma A\bar x^k)\). The diagonal scaling is admissible under the strict coupling condition \(\|\Sigma^{1/2}AT^{1/2}\|_2<1\), equivalently \(T^{-1}-A^\top\Sigma A\succ0\). Cone projections must be evaluated in the \(T^{-1}\)-metric when the primal proximal term contains a cone indicator.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Use positive diagonal primal and dual step matrices, constrained so the diagonally scaled coupling operator has norm below one.
assumptions_latex: \(T\) and \(\Sigma\) are positive diagonal matrices.
The required metric proximal maps are computable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T^{-1}-A^\top\Sigma A\succ0\).

notation.meaning: proximal map of h in metric M

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition kind is defensible for this preconditioning leaf, and the norm and Schur-complement conditions are consistent for positive-definite metrics. No source supports the precise metric-proximal convention or the implementation claim concerning cone projections.

knowledge_statements.title: Block-Metric PDHG
knowledge_statements.scope_note: PDHG with positive-definite block metrics matched to product-space conic structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\min_x f(x)+g(Ax)\), partition the primal and dual spaces into blocks and choose self-adjoint block-diagonal operators \(T\succ0\) and \(\Sigma\succ0\). Initialize \(x^0,y^0\) and \(\bar x^0=x^0\). Iterate \(y^{k+1}=\operatorname{prox}_{g^*}^{\Sigma^{-1}}(y^k+\Sigma A\bar x^k)\), \(x^{k+1}=\operatorname{prox}_{f}^{T^{-1}}(x^k-TA^\top y^{k+1})\), and \(\bar x^{k+1}=x^{k+1}+\theta(x^{k+1}-x^k)\). Require \(\|\Sigma^{1/2}AT^{1/2}\|_2<1\). Stop by primal–dual residual tolerances and return \((x^{k+1},y^{k+1})\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Run PDHG in block-diagonal primal and dual metrics, allowing separate scaling of structured variable and constraint blocks.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) and \(g\) are proper, closed, and convex.
\(T\) and \(\Sigma\) are self-adjoint positive-definite block-diagonal operators.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T^{-1}-A^\top\Sigma A\succ0\) is an equivalent strict metric-coupling condition.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits Block-Metric PDHG, but no source supports the stated update ordering and strict metric condition. The record also introduces theta without specifying its domain in either the statement or assumptions, so the exact algorithmic variant cannot be validated.

knowledge_statements.title: Residual-Balancing PDHG
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Adaptive PDHG scaling that balances normalized primal and dual residuals while preserving the step-size product.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(p^k\geq0\) and \(d^k\geq0\) be normalized primal and dual residual norms after a PDHG iteration. Fix \(\mu>1\), \(\eta>1\), and step sizes \(\tau_k,\sigma_k>0\). If \(p^k>\mu d^k\), set \(\tau_{k+1}=\tau_k/\eta\) and \(\sigma_{k+1}=\eta\sigma_k\); if \(d^k>\mu p^k\), set \(\tau_{k+1}=\eta\tau_k\) and \(\sigma_{k+1}=\sigma_k/\eta\); otherwise leave both unchanged. Continue PDHG with the updated steps and stop when both residuals meet tolerance. The update preserves \(\tau_{k+1}\sigma_{k+1}=\tau_k\sigma_k\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At iteration \(k\), choose trial steps \(\tau>0\) and \(\sigma>0\), compute the corresponding PDHG candidates \(y^+=\operatorname{prox}_{g^*}^{\sigma^{-1}I}(y^k+\sigma A\bar x^k)\) and \(x^+=\operatorname{prox}_{f}^{\tau^{-1}I}(x^k-\tau A^\top y^+)\). \(A\) is linear and the displayed proximal maps are computable.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Stacked-operator lifting of multiple block constraints into one product-space constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(T:H\to G_1\times\cdots\times G_m\) and \(C\) by \[Tx=(T_1x,\ldots,T_mx),\qquad C=C_1\times\cdots\times C_m.\] Then \[T_ix\in C_i\ \text{for every }i\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad Tx\in C,\] and the indicator composition satisfies \[\delta_C(Tx)=\sum_{i=1}^m\delta_{C_i}(T_ix).\] Moreover, the adjoint is \(T^*(y_1,\ldots,y_m)=\sum_{i=1}^mT_i^*y_i\). Thus blockwise primal or dual contributions can be evaluated independently, while the stacked adjoint aggregates them into the original variable space.

knowledge_statements.title: Alternating-Projection Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convergence for two consistent closed convex sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \[x^{k+1}=P_C(P_Dx^k),\qquad k=0,1,\ldots.\] Then there exists \(x^\star\in C\cap D\) such that \(x^k\to x^\star\). Equivalently, \(\operatorname{dist}(x^k,C\cap D)\to0\), and the interprojection residual satisfies \(\|P_Dx^k-x^{k+1}\|\to0\). The conclusion asserts convergence to some feasible point; except for special geometric cases, it does not assert that the limit equals the metric projection \(P_{C\cap D}x^0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For two closed convex sets with nonempty intersection in finite dimensions, repeated alternating projections converge to a feasible point.
assumptions_latex: \(C,D\) are nonempty closed convex subsets of a finite-dimensional Hilbert space.
The intersection \(C\cap D\) is nonempty.
The initial point \(x^0\) is arbitrary.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The alternating-projection sequence converges to a point of \(C\cap D\), and its distance to the intersection tends to zero.

knowledge_statements.title: Dykstra Projection Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cyclic Dykstra algorithm for projecting onto a finite intersection of convex sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(x=a\) and \(p_i=0\) for \(i=1,\ldots,m\). During each cycle and for \(i=1,\ldots,m\), perform \[y=P_{C_i}(x+p_i),\qquad p_i\leftarrow x+p_i-y,\qquad x\leftarrow y.\] Repeat complete cycles until successive primal iterates and the constraint violations meet tolerance, then return \(x\). If \(C=\bigcap_{i=1}^m C_i\neq\varnothing\), the primal iterates at the ends of cycles converge to the unique point \[P_Ca=\mathop{\arg\min}_{u\in C}\frac12\|u-a\|^2.\] The correction vectors distinguish Dykstra's metric projection method from uncorrected cyclic alternating projections.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dykstra's method cycles through set projections while updating correction vectors, and converges to the nearest point in the intersection.
assumptions_latex: \(C_1,\ldots,C_m\) are nonempty closed convex subsets of a finite-dimensional Hilbert space with nonempty intersection.
The initial primal point is \(x^0=a\), and correction vectors satisfy \(p_i^0=0\).
Projections onto all \(C_i\) are available.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The cyclic Dykstra iterates converge to the metric projection \(P_{\cap_i C_i}a\).

knowledge_statements.title: Consistent-Feasibility Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional Douglas–Rachford convergence for a consistent two-set feasibility problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Starting from arbitrary \(z^0\), generate \[z^{k+1}=T_\lambda z^k,\qquad T_\lambda=(1-\lambda/2)I+(\lambda/2)R_DR_C.\] Then \(z^k\) converges to some \(z^\star\in\operatorname{Fix}T_\lambda\). Its shadow satisfies \[P_Cz^\star\in C\cap D,\] and \(P_Cz^k\to P_Cz^\star\). Moreover, the fixed-point residual \(\|T_\lambda z^k-z^k\|\) tends to zero. Thus consistency is diagnosed through convergence of the shadow to a common feasible point, whereas the fixed point itself need not belong to either set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With two intersecting closed convex sets, relaxed Douglas–Rachford iterates converge to a fixed point whose projection shadow is feasible.
assumptions_latex: \(C,D\) are nonempty closed convex subsets of a finite-dimensional Hilbert space.
The feasibility problem is consistent: \(C\cap D\neq\varnothing\).
The relaxation satisfies \(0<\lambda<2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The Douglas–Rachford iterates converge to a fixed point, and their projection shadows converge to a point in \(C\cap D\).

notation.meaning: reflection across a closed convex set S

knowledge_statements.title: Inconsistent-Feasibility Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete disjoint-set example separating consistent fixed-point behavior from infeasibility displacement behavior.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(C=\{0\}\) and \(D=\{d\}\) with \(d\neq0\), the sets are disjoint. Their reflections satisfy \(R_Cz=-z\) and \(R_Dw=2d-w\), so \[Tz=\frac12\bigl(z+R_DR_Cz\bigr)=z+d.\] Consequently, \[z^k=z^0+kd,\qquad z^{k+1}-z^k=d,\] and \(\operatorname{Fix}T=\varnothing\). Thus removing consistency destroys fixed-point convergence even for singleton closed convex sets. The persistent displacement has norm \(\|d\|=\operatorname{dist}(C,D)\), while the projection shadows remain the best-approximation pair \((0,d)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For two distinct singleton sets, Douglas–Rachford iterates drift by their separation vector, so fixed-point convergence fails while displacement reveals inconsistency.
assumptions_latex: The ambient space is Euclidean and \(C=\{0\}\), \(D=\{d\}\) for a fixed nonzero vector \(d\).
Douglas–Rachford uses \(T=\tfrac12(I+R_DR_C)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The inconsistent pair has no Douglas–Rachford fixed point; the iterates translate by \(d\) and diverge although their displacement exactly records the feasibility gap.

knowledge_statements.title: Primal–Dual Projection Conversion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Moreau conversion between Euclidean projections onto a closed convex cone and its dual cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\) be a nonempty closed convex cone in a finite-dimensional real Hilbert space, and define \(K^*=\{y:\langle y,x\rangle\ge 0\ \text{for every }x\in K\}\). knowledge_statements.title: Parallel Cone Projection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Independent projection of product-cone blocks on parallel workers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a product cone \(K=K_1\times\cdots\times K_m\) and a conformally partitioned vector \(z=(z_1,\ldots,z_m)\). After all assigned projections finish, return \(p=(p_1,\ldots,p_m)\). Orthogonality of the product norm implies \[p=\Pi_K(z),\qquad \|p-z\|^2=\sum_{i=1}^m\|p_i-z_i\|^2.\] No synchronization is mathematically required before the final assembly.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Vectorized evaluation of one cone-projection oracle on multiple inputs.

knowledge_statements.title: Zero-Cone Projection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact Euclidean projection onto the zero cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the zero cone \(K_0=\{0\}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), the feasible set contains only the origin. Hence, for every \(z\in\mathbb{R}^n\), \[\Pi_{K_0}(z)=\mathop{\operatorname{argmin}}_{x\in K_0}\|x-z\|^2=0,\qquad \operatorname{dist}(z,K_0)=\|z\|.\] Thus a zero-cone projection block discards its input and returns a zero vector of the same dimension.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projection onto the zero cone always returns the origin, and the projection distance equals the norm of the input.
assumptions_latex: \(z\in\mathbb{R}^n\).
Distance and projection use the Euclidean norm.

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projection onto the free cone is the identity map, and every input has zero distance from the cone.

knowledge_statements.title: Zero–Free Dual Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dual and polar relationships between the zero and free cones.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In \(\mathbb{R}^n\), define the dual cone by \(K^*=\{y:\langle y,x\rangle\ge0\ \text{for every }x\in K\}\) and the polar cone by \(K^\circ=-K^*\). Then \[\{0\}^*=\mathbb{R}^n,\qquad (\mathbb{R}^n)^*=\{0\},\qquad \{0\}^\circ=\mathbb{R}^n,\qquad (\mathbb{R}^n)^\circ=\{0\}.\] Accordingly, the zero and free cones form a dual pair, and their projection maps are respectively the zero and identity operators.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The zero cone and full space are dual to each other; their projection maps are respectively zero and identity.

children.title: Orthant Projection

knowledge_statements.title: Orthant Projection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinatewise Euclidean projection onto the nonnegative orthant.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the nonnegative orthant \(K_+=\mathbb{R}_+^n\) and any \(z\in\mathbb{R}^n\), the Euclidean projection separates by coordinate: \[\Pi_{K_+}(z)=z_+,
\qquad (z_+)_i=\max\{z_i,0\},\quad i=1,\ldots,n.\] The residual is \(z-z_+=z_-\), where \((z_-)_i=\min\{z_i,0\}\), and \(\langle z_+,z_-\rangle=0\). Thus projection requires only coordinatewise thresholding.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projecting onto the nonnegative orthant replaces every negative coordinate by zero and leaves every nonnegative coordinate unchanged.
assumptions_latex: \(z\in\mathbb{R}^n\).
Projection uses the Euclidean norm.

children.title: Box-Cone Projection
children.top_down_role: Projection regimes for conic representations of bound constraints.

knowledge_statements.title: Box-Cone Projection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Projection onto the homogenized cone generated by a finite axis-aligned box.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(l,u\in\mathbb{R}^n\) satisfy \(l_i\le u_i\), and define \(K_{l,u}=\{(\tau,x):\tau\ge0,\ \tau l\le x\le\tau u\}\). For input \((t,z)\), define \(x_i(\tau)=\min\{\max\{z_i,\tau l_i\},\tau u_i\}\). Then \[\tau^*\in\mathop{\operatorname{argmin}}_{\tau\ge0}\left((\tau-t)^2+\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i(\tau)-z_i)^2\right),\qquad \Pi_{K_{l,u}}(t,z)=(\tau^*,x(\tau^*)).\] The scalar objective is convex and piecewise quadratic, and the projected vector is obtained by coordinatewise clipping once \(\tau^*\) is known.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projection onto a homogenized box cone reduces to one convex scalar minimization followed by coordinatewise clipping to the scaled box.
assumptions_latex: \(l,u\in\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(l_i\le u_i\) for every \(i\).
Projection uses the Euclidean product norm.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Pi_{K_{l,u}}(t,z)=(\tau^*,x(\tau^*))\) with \(\tau^*\) determined by the displayed scalar minimization.

notation.meaning: Homogenized cone over the axis-aligned box from l to u.

knowledge_statements.title: Orthant-to-Box Specialization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinatewise clipping unifies orthant and axis-aligned box projections.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For extended bounds \(l_i\in\mathbb{R}\cup\{-\infty\}\) and \(u_i\in\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) satisfying \(l_i\le u_i\), let \(B(l,u)=\{x:l_i\le x_i\le u_i\}\). Its Euclidean projection is \[(\Pi_{B(l,u)}z)_i=\min\{\max\{z_i,l_i\},u_i\}.\] Choosing \(l_i=0\) and \(u_i=+\infty\) for every \(i\) specializes this formula to \((\Pi_{\mathbb{R}_+^n}z)_i=\max\{z_i,0\}\). Thus orthant projection is the one-sided unbounded-box case of coordinatewise box projection.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Coordinatewise box clipping becomes nonnegative-orthant projection when every lower bound is zero and every upper bound is infinite.

Projection uses the Euclidean norm.

knowledge_statements.title: General Polyhedral Projection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quadratic-program representation and optimality certificate for projection onto a polyhedral cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax\le0\}\) be a nonempty polyhedral cone. For every \(z\in\mathbb{R}^n\), its Euclidean projection is the unique solution of \[\Pi_K(z)=\mathop{\operatorname{argmin}}_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n}\left\{\tfrac12\|x-z\|^2:Ax\le0\right\}.\] A pair \((x,\lambda)\) solves this projection problem exactly if \[Ax\le0,\qquad \lambda\ge0,\qquad x-z+A^{\mathsf T}\lambda=0,\qquad \lambda_i(Ax)_i=0\ \text{for every }i.\] Hence a general polyhedral-cone projection can be computed as a strongly convex quadratic program and checked through these conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projection onto a polyhedral cone is a strongly convex quadratic program whose solution is certified by primal feasibility, stationarity, dual feasibility, and complementarity.
assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\).
\(K=\{x:Ax\le0\}\) is nonempty.
Projection uses the Euclidean norm.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x=\Pi_K(z)\) exactly when there exists \(\lambda\) satisfying the displayed optimality conditions.

knowledge_statements.title: Lorentz-Cone Projection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closed-form Euclidean projection onto the standard Lorentz cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(L_{n+1}=\{(t,x)\in\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}^n:\|x\|_2\le t\}\), and set \(r=\|x\|_2\). Its Euclidean projection is \[\Pi_{L_{n+1}}(t,x)=\begin{cases}(t,x),&r\le t,\\(0,0),&r\le -t,\\\left(\dfrac{t+r}{2},\dfrac{t+r}{2r}x\right),&|t|<r.\end{cases}\] The three cases respectively correspond to an input inside the cone, inside the negative cone, and between those regions. In the third case \(r>0\), so the displayed division is well defined.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Lorentz-cone projection is identity inside the cone, zero inside its negative, and otherwise has a closed-form boundary projection.
assumptions_latex: \((t,x)\in\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}^n\).
Projection uses the standard Euclidean norm.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Pi_{L_{n+1}}(t,x)\) is given by the displayed three-regime formula.

notation.meaning: Euclidean norm of the vector component x.

knowledge_statements.title: Rotated Second-Order-Cone Projection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Euclidean projection obtained by an orthogonal transformation to the Lorentz cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(K_{\mathrm r}=\{(u,v,w)\in\mathbb R\times\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n:u\geq0,\ v\geq0,\ 2uv\geq\lVert w\rVert_2^2\}\). Let \(T(u,v,w)=((u+v)/\sqrt2,(u-v)/\sqrt2,w)\) and \(L_{n+2}=\{(t,z):t\geq\lVert z\rVert_2\}\). Since \(T\) is orthogonal and \(T(K_{\mathrm r})=L_{n+2}\), compute the projection of \(a\) by \[\Pi_{K_{\mathrm r}}(a)=T^{-1}\!\left(\Pi_{L_{n+2}}(Ta)\right).\] The Lorentz-cone projection uses its interior, boundary, and apex formulas and returns the unique Euclidean nearest point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Transform the rotated cone orthogonally into a Lorentz cone, apply the standard Lorentz-cone projection, and transform the result back.
assumptions_latex: Projection is taken in the standard Euclidean norm.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Pi_{K_{\mathrm r}}=T^{-1}\circ\Pi_{L_{n+2}}\circ T\).

children.title: Boundary Projection Regime
children.top_down_role: Second-order-cone projection behavior at nonapical boundary points.

knowledge_statements.title: Boundary Projection Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The nontrivial Lorentz-cone regime whose projection lies on the curved boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(L_{n+1}=\{(t,x)\in\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n:t\geq\lVert x\rVert_2\}\), let \(a=(t,x)\), and set \(r=\lVert x\rVert_2\). The boundary projection regime is the predicate \(-r<t<r\), which implies \(r>0\). In this regime the Euclidean projection is \[\Pi_{L_{n+1}}(t,x)=\left(\frac{t+r}{2},\frac{t+r}{2r}x\right).\] Its two components have equal scalar and vector norms, so the projected point is nonzero and belongs to \(\partial L_{n+1}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When the scalar coordinate lies strictly between minus and plus the vector norm, projection lands nontrivially on the Lorentz-cone boundary.
assumptions_latex: \(a=(t,x)\in\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n\).
\(-\lVert x\rVert_2<t<\lVert x\rVert_2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Pi_{L_{n+1}}(a)\in\partial L_{n+1}\setminus\{0\}\).

notation.meaning: the norm of the vector component

children.title: Apex Projection Regime
children.top_down_role: Second-order-cone projection behavior near the cone apex.

knowledge_statements.title: Apex Projection Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The Lorentz-cone regime in which the nearest feasible point is the apex.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(L_{n+1}=\{(t,x)\in\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n:t\geq\lVert x\rVert_2\}\), a point \(a=(t,x)\) is in the apex projection regime exactly when \(t\leq-\lVert x\rVert_2\), equivalently \(a\in-L_{n+1}\). Because the Lorentz cone is self-dual, this condition places \(a\) in its polar cone. Consequently, \[\Pi_{L_{n+1}}(a)=(0,0).\] Equality is included and forms the transition from the curved-boundary formula to the apex formula.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A point projects to the Lorentz-cone apex exactly when its scalar coordinate is no greater than minus the vector norm.
assumptions_latex: \(a=(t,x)\in\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(t\leq-\lVert x\rVert_2\Longleftrightarrow\Pi_{L_{n+1}}(a)=0\).

notation.meaning: Euclidean projection onto the Lorentz cone

children.title: Boundary-to-Apex Transition
children.top_down_role: Sensitivity and classification changes as projected points approach the apex.

knowledge_statements.title: Boundary-to-Apex Transition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The switching surface between nonzero boundary projection and apex projection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(a=(t,x)\), \(r=\lVert x\rVert_2>0\), and \(L_{n+1}=\{(s,z):s\geq\lVert z\rVert_2\}\). The boundary-to-apex transition is the hypersurface \(t=-r\). Substitution into the boundary formula gives \[\left(\frac{t+r}{2},\frac{t+r}{2r}x\right)=(0,0),\] agreeing with the apex formula. Thus \(\Pi_{L_{n+1}}\) is continuous across the transition, but it is not differentiable there: on the side \(t<-r\) it is locally constant, whereas on the side \(-r<t<r\) it has a nonzero directional response.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At scalar coordinate minus the vector norm, the boundary formula collapses continuously to the apex, while differentiability fails across the switch.
assumptions_latex: Projection is Euclidean.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(t=-\lVert x\rVert_2\) is a continuous but nondifferentiable regime boundary.

notation.meaning: the norm of the vector component

knowledge_statements.title: Full Spectral PSD Projection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact Frobenius projection of a real symmetric matrix onto the PSD cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(X\in\mathbb S^n\), compute a complete orthogonal eigendecomposition \(X=Q\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_n)Q^\top\). A numerical implementation stops after the full symmetric eigensolver meets its prescribed backward-error tolerance and reports \(X_+\), optionally symmetrized against roundoff.

knowledge_statements.title: Partial-Spectrum PSD Projection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: PSD projection reconstructed from only the computed positive spectral subspace.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\in\mathbb S^n\). Compute orthonormal eigenpairs \((\lambda_i,q_i)\) only for an index set \(I\) containing every positive eigenvalue, and return \[\widehat X_+=\sum_{i\in I}(\lambda_i)_+q_iq_i^\top.\] The result equals the exact PSD projection if every omitted eigenvalue is nonpositive. More generally, if the computed eigenpairs are exact, \[\lVert\Pi_{\mathbb S_+^n}(X)-\widehat X_+\rVert_F^2=\sum_{i\notin I}(\lambda_i)_+^2.\] An eigensolver may stop once a certified upper bound for every uncomputed eigenvalue is nonpositive, or when the displayed residual error meets a chosen tolerance.

Computed eigenvectors are orthonormal.

knowledge_statements.title: Low-Rank PSD Projection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Frobenius projection onto PSD matrices whose rank is bounded by a prescribed integer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\in\mathbb S^n\) have eigenvalues \(\lambda_1\geq\cdots\geq\lambda_n\) with corresponding orthonormal eigenvectors \(q_i\), and fix \(0\leq r\leq n\). Return \[Y_r=\sum_{i=1}^{r}(\lambda_i)_+q_iq_i^\top.\] Then \(Y_r\) solves \[\min\{\lVert X-Y\rVert_F:Y\succeq0,\ \operatorname{rank}(Y)\leq r\}.\] The minimizer is unique when the retained positive eigenspace is separated from the discarded spectrum; a positive eigenvalue tie across the rank cutoff can make the projection set-valued.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Y_r\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{Y\succeq0,\,\operatorname{rank}(Y)\leq r}\lVert X-Y\rVert_F\).

children.title: Clustered Eigenvalue Regimes

knowledge_statements.title: Clustered Eigenvalue Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Stability distinction between invariant spectral projectors and individual eigenvectors inside a cluster.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\in\mathbb S^n\) have an eigenvalue cluster indexed by \(I\), and suppose the cluster is separated from the remaining spectrum by \(\delta=\min_{i\in I,j\notin I}|\lambda_i-\lambda_j|>0\). The invariant projector \(P_I=\sum_{i\in I}q_iq_i^\top\) is uniquely defined and stable under perturbations small relative to \(\delta\), even when eigenvalues within the cluster coincide. Individual eigenvectors inside a repeated cluster are not unique and may rotate arbitrarily. For PSD projection, such rotations do not affect the reconstructed matrix when the clustered eigenvalues receive the same scalar positive-part transformation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Separated clustered eigenspaces are stable as subspaces, but their individual eigenvectors can be nonunique; equal spectral clipping makes those rotations irrelevant.
assumptions_latex: The cluster-to-complement gap satisfies \(\delta>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_I\) is basis invariant, whereas the individual \(q_i\) for \(i\in I\) need not be.

notation.meaning: orthogonal projector onto the clustered invariant subspace

children.title: Near-Zero Eigenvalue Regimes

assumptions_latex: \(X,E\in\mathbb S^n\).
The eigenvalues are indexed in nonincreasing order.
The perturbation satisfies \(\lVert E\rVert_2\leq\eta\) for a specified \(\eta\geq0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(|\lambda_i(X)|>\eta\), then every admissible perturbation preserves the sign of \(\lambda_i\); if \(|\lambda_i(X)|\leq\eta\), the eigenvalue can be moved to zero, and if \(|\lambda_i(X)|<\eta\), it can be moved across zero. In all cases, \(\lVert\Pi_{\mathbb S_+^n}(X+E)-\Pi_{\mathbb S_+^n}(X)\rVert_F\leq\lVert E\rVert_F\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale:Weyl eigenvalue perturbation bound, explicit rank-one perturbations, and nonexpansiveness of convex projection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Numerical sign classification and projected rank become fragile when eigenvalues approach the PSD clipping threshold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\in\mathbb S^n\), let \(E\in\mathbb S^n\) satisfy \(\lVert E\rVert_2\leq\eta\), and index eigenvalues in nonincreasing order. Weyl's bound gives \[|\lambda_i(X+E)-\lambda_i(X)|\leq\lVert E\rVert_2\leq\eta.\] Hence \(|\lambda_i(X)|>\eta\) guarantees that every admissible perturbation preserves the sign of \(\lambda_i\). If \(|\lambda_i(X)|\leq\eta\), a symmetric rank-one perturbation along an eigenvector can move that eigenvalue to zero; if \(|\lambda_i(X)|<\eta\), such a perturbation can move it across zero. Thus the rank of \(\Pi_{\mathbb S_+^n}(X)\) can change under arbitrarily small perturbations along sequences for which a nonzero eigenvalue approaches zero. Nevertheless, Euclidean projection onto the closed convex cone \(\mathbb S_+^n\) is nonexpansive, so \[\lVert\Pi_{\mathbb S_+^n}(X+E)-\Pi_{\mathbb S_+^n}(X)\rVert_F\leq\lVert E\rVert_F.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A perturbation bound preserves an eigenvalue's sign only when the eigenvalue is farther from zero than the bound. At or inside that threshold it can reach zero, and strictly inside it can cross zero, although the full PSD projection remains nonexpansive.

children.title: Spectral-Gap Failure Boundary
children.top_down_role: Reliability limits associated with weak separation around the PSD threshold.

knowledge_statements.title: Spectral-Gap Failure Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Loss of a cutoff gap makes rank-truncated PSD projection nonunique and branch-sensitive.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the rank-one PSD projection of \(X_\varepsilon=\operatorname{diag}(1+\varepsilon,1-\varepsilon,0)\). For \(\varepsilon>0\), its unique solution is \(Y_\varepsilon=\operatorname{diag}(1+\varepsilon,0,0)\); for \(\varepsilon<0\), its unique solution is \(Y_\varepsilon=\operatorname{diag}(0,1-\varepsilon,0)\). At \(\varepsilon=0\), the leading eigenvalue has multiplicity two, the cutoff gap vanishes, and every matrix \(uu^\top\) with \(u\in\operatorname{span}\{e_1,e_2\}\) and \(\lVert u\rVert_2=1\) is optimal. Thus no continuous single-valued choice can agree with both unique branches.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When the eigenvalue gap at a rank cutoff closes, the truncated PSD projection becomes nonunique and selections from opposite sides need not converge together.
assumptions_latex: Projection is onto \(\{Y\succeq0:\operatorname{rank}(Y)\leq1\}\) in Frobenius norm.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The rank-one projection is set-valued at \(\varepsilon=0\) and admits incompatible one-sided selections.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale:direct spectral calculation for a diagonal matrix family

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The diagonal family correctly exhibits nonuniqueness when the rank-cutoff gap closes, and counterexample is an appropriate role for this concrete failure witness. No external source or registered internal verification is supplied.
