knowledge_statements.title: Primal Exponential-Cone Projection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Euclidean projection onto the closed primal exponential cone, including its nonsmooth face.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(K_{\exp}=\operatorname{cl}\{(x,y,z):y>0,\ y\exp(x/y)\leq z\}\). For \(a=(r,s,t)\in\mathbb R^3\), the primal projection is the unique minimizer \[\Pi_{K_{\exp}}(a)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{(x,y,z)\in K_{\exp}}\frac12\bigl((x-r)^2+(y-s)^2+(z-t)^2\bigr).\] The closure adds the face \(F=\{(x,0,z):x\leq0,\ z\geq0\}\). A smooth-boundary candidate satisfies \(y>0\), \(z=y\exp(x/y)\), and, for some \(\mu\geq0\), \[(x-r,y-s,z-t)+\mu\bigl(e^{x/y},e^{x/y}(1-x/y),-1\bigr)=0.\] The projection is the nearest feasible candidate from the interior, \(F\), or this KKT system.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The primal exponential-cone projection is a unique nearest point, found by comparing interior, closure-face, and smooth-boundary KKT candidates.
assumptions_latex: \(a\in\mathbb R^3\).
Distance is Euclidean.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Pi_{K_{\exp}}(a)\) exists uniquely and obeys the displayed boundary system whenever it lies on the smooth boundary.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale:closed convex projection and boundary KKT conditions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The closed-cone definition, closure face, projection representation, and smooth-boundary KKT system are internally consistent, and representation fits the record's mathematical role. An authoritative exponential-cone projection source with a specific locator is required.

children.title: Dual Exponential-Cone Projection
children.top_down_role: Projection onto the dual exponential cone.

knowledge_statements.title: Dual Exponential-Cone Projection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Computes the Euclidean projection onto the dual exponential cone through a primal-cone oracle.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(K_{\exp}=\operatorname{cl}\{(x,y,z):y>0,\ y\exp(x/y)\le z\}\) and \(K_{\exp}^{*}=\{s:\langle s,x\rangle\ge0\ \forall x\in K_{\exp}\}\). For input \(q\in\mathbb R^{3}\), compute \(p=\Pi_{K_{\exp}}(-q)\) and return \(q+p\). Moreau decomposition gives
\[\Pi_{K_{\exp}^{*}}(q)=q+\Pi_{K_{\exp}}(-q).\]
The returned point is the unique minimizer of \(\tfrac12\|s-q\|_2^2\) over \(s\in K_{\exp}^{*}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Project the negated input onto the primal exponential cone, add the original input, and obtain its unique dual-cone projection.
assumptions_latex: \(q\in\mathbb R^3\)
The primal projection oracle returns the exact Euclidean projection.

notation.meaning: Euclidean projection onto a closed convex set C

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm and dual-projection identity are mathematically consistent and fit the terminal container, but no inspectable source supports the Moreau conversion or exponential-cone convention.

knowledge_statements.title: Polar Exponential-Cone Projection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Computes projection onto the nonpositive-inner-product polar of the exponential cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(K_{\exp}=\operatorname{cl}\{(x,y,z):y>0,\ y\exp(x/y)\le z\}\) and \(K_{\exp}^{\circ}=\{s:\langle s,x\rangle\le0\ \forall x\in K_{\exp}\}\). Given \(q\in\mathbb R^3\), compute \(p=\Pi_{K_{\exp}}(q)\) and return \(q-p\). Moreau decomposition yields
\[\Pi_{K_{\exp}^{\circ}}(q)=q-\Pi_{K_{\exp}}(q),\qquad \langle p,q-p\rangle=0.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Subtract the primal exponential-cone projection from the input; the residual is its unique polar-cone projection and is orthogonal to the primal component.
assumptions_latex: \(q\in\mathbb R^3\)
The primal projection oracle returns the exact Euclidean projection.

notation.meaning: polar exponential cone under the nonpositive convention

knowledge_statements.title: Dual–Polar Projection Conversion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fixes the sign conversion between dual and polar exponential-cone projection oracles.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every nonempty closed convex cone \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), define \(K^*=\{y:\langle y,x\rangle\ge0\ \forall x\in K\}\) and \(K^\circ=\{y:\langle y,x\rangle\le0\ \forall x\in K\}\). Then \(K^\circ=-K^*\), and for every \(q\in\mathbb R^n\),
\[\Pi_{K^*}(q)=-\Pi_{K^\circ}(-q),\qquad \Pi_{K^\circ}(q)=-\Pi_{K^*}(-q).\]
These identities apply in particular to \(K=K_{\exp}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dual and polar cones differ by a sign, so either projection oracle is obtained from the other by negating both input and output.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is a nonempty closed convex cone.
Euclidean projection is used.

notation.meaning: dual cone with nonnegative inner products
polar cone with nonpositive inner products

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The cited polar-and-dual-cones section may support the sign relation, but the locator does not specifically support the Euclidean projection identities. A Moreau decomposition or projection locator is required.

knowledge_statements.title: Root-Finding Projection Mechanisms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Interior exponential-cone projection reduced to a scalar root, with separate face candidates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(q=(a,b,c)\notin K_{\exp}\cup K_{\exp}^{\circ}\), seek a smooth-boundary projection using \(r=x/y\). Define
\[\lambda(r)=\frac{a-rb}{e^r(1-r+r^2)},\quad y(r)=b-\lambda(r)e^r(1-r),\quad F(r)=y(r)e^r-c-\lambda(r).\]
Find a root \(r\) satisfying \(\lambda(r)>0\) and \(y(r)>0\), then set \(x=ry(r)\) and \(z=c+\lambda(r)\). Compare this candidate with projections onto the closed face \(\{(x,0,z):x\le0,\ z\ge0\}\), and return the feasible candidate of least squared distance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A smooth exponential-cone projection follows from one scalar root; face candidates must also be checked to cover nonsmooth boundary cases.
assumptions_latex: \(q=(a,b,c)\in\mathbb R^3\)
\(K_{\exp}=\operatorname{cl}\{(x,y,z):y>0,\ y e^{x/y}\le z\}\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The least-distance admissible candidate equals \(\Pi_{K_{\exp}}(q)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The scalar equations are plausible KKT reductions and the algorithm kind fits, but the root conditions and assertion that the listed candidates exhaust all projection regimes require an authoritative source.

knowledge_statements.title: Exponential-Projection Boundary Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Partitions exponential-cone projection into membership, polar, smooth-boundary, and closed-face regimes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(q=(a,b,c)\in\mathbb R^3\), first return \(q\) if \(q\in K_{\exp}\), and return \(0\) if \(q\in K_{\exp}^{\circ}\). Otherwise form the smooth-boundary candidate from the exponential-cone KKT equations and the face candidate
\[p_F=(\min\{a,0\},0,\max\{c,0\})\in F,\qquad F=\{(x,0,z):x\le0,\ z\ge0\}.\]
Discard any candidate violating its regime conditions and return the remaining candidate minimizing \(\|p-q\|_2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Membership and polar tests handle trivial projections; all other inputs require comparison between the smooth exponential boundary and the cone's closed face.
assumptions_latex: \(K_{\exp}=\operatorname{cl}\{(x,y,z):y>0,\ y e^{x/y}\le z\}\)
All candidate distances are evaluated in the Euclidean norm.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The selected candidate is \(\Pi_{K_{\exp}}(q)\).

notation.meaning: the y=0 face of the exponential cone
Euclidean projection of q onto F

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The membership, polar, and face formulas are plausible, but no source establishes that the stated regime partition and candidate comparison are complete.

knowledge_statements.title: Three-Dimensional Power-Cone Projection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: KKT-based Euclidean projection onto the scalar three-dimensional power cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Fix \(0<\alpha<1\), put \(\beta=1-\alpha\), and define \(K_\alpha=\{(x,y,z):x\ge0,\ y\ge0,\ |z|\le x^\alpha y^\beta\}\). For input \((a,b,c)\), apply membership and polar tests first. Otherwise seek \(\lambda\ge0\), \(x>0\), \(y>0\), and \(w\ge0\) satisfying
\[x=a+\lambda\alpha w/x,\quad y=b+\lambda\beta w/y,\quad w=|c|-\lambda,\quad w=x^\alpha y^\beta.\]
Set \(z=\operatorname{sgn}(c)w\), compare with applicable face candidates, and return the feasible candidate of minimum distance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Project onto a three-dimensional power cone by membership tests, a boundary KKT solve, and comparison with lower-dimensional face candidates.
assumptions_latex: The nonlinear system is solved over its stated nonnegative domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The minimum-distance candidate equals \(\Pi_{K_\alpha}(a,b,c)\).

notation.meaning: absolute value of the projected third coordinate

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The boundary KKT system is plausible and the algorithm kind matches the projection container, but the applicable face candidates are not specified and neither correctness nor completeness is sourced.

knowledge_statements.title: Dual Power-Cone Projection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dual power-cone projection obtained from the primal projection by Moreau decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(0<\alpha<1\), let \(K_\alpha=\{(x,y,z):x\ge0,\ y\ge0,\ |z|\le x^\alpha y^{1-\alpha}\}\). Its nonnegative-inner-product dual is
\[K_\alpha^*=\{(u,v,w):u\ge0,\ v\ge0,\ |w|\le(u/\alpha)^\alpha(v/(1-\alpha))^{1-\alpha}\}.\]
Given \(q\in\mathbb R^3\), compute \(p=\Pi_{K_\alpha}(-q)\) and return \(q+p\). Then \(q+p=\Pi_{K_\alpha^*}(q)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The dual power cone has a scaled geometric-mean inequality, and its projection is the input plus the primal projection of the negated input.
assumptions_latex: The dual uses the nonnegative-inner-product convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Pi_{K_\alpha^*}(q)=q+\Pi_{K_\alpha}(-q)\)

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed dual cone and Moreau-based projection conversion are mathematically plausible and locally appropriate, but both nontrivial claims lack cited support.

knowledge_statements.title: Generalized Power-Cone Projection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar-root mechanism for the vector-valued generalized power cone away from its faces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\alpha_i>0\), \(\sum_{i=1}^m\alpha_i=1\), and \(K_\alpha=\{(x,z):x\in\mathbb R_+^m,\ \|z\|_2\le\prod_i x_i^{\alpha_i}\}\). For input \((a,c)\), put \(\rho=\|c\|_2\). After membership and polar tests, solve for \(0\le\lambda\le\rho\):
\[t=\rho-\lambda,\quad x_i=\frac{a_i+\sqrt{a_i^2+4\lambda\alpha_i t}}2,\quad t=\prod_i x_i^{\alpha_i}.\]
If \(\rho>0\), set \(z=(t/\rho)c\). Compare this smooth candidate with applicable face candidates and return the nearest feasible one.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A generalized power-cone projection reduces its smooth case to one multiplier equation, followed by comparison with candidates on coordinate faces.
assumptions_latex: \(\alpha_i>0\) and \(\sum_i\alpha_i=1\)
The smooth formula is used only when its computed coordinates are positive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The least-distance feasible candidate is \(\Pi_{K_\alpha}(a,c)\).

notation.meaning: norm of the projected vector block

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The smooth scalar reduction is plausible, but the unspecified coordinate-face candidates make the algorithm incomplete as stated, and no source validates the formula or candidate exhaustiveness.

knowledge_statements.title: Extreme-Exponent Projection Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identifies limiting cones and numerical degeneration as a power-cone exponent approaches zero or one.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(K_\alpha=\{(x,y,z):x\ge0,\ y\ge0,\ |z|\le x^\alpha y^{1-\alpha}\}\), the closed-cone limits are
\[K_\alpha\to K_0=\{(x,y,z):x\ge0,\ y\ge|z|\}\quad(\alpha\downarrow0),\]
\[K_\alpha\to K_1=\{(x,y,z):y\ge0,\ x\ge|z|\}\quad(\alpha\uparrow1).\]
Accordingly, fixed-input Euclidean projections converge to the corresponding limiting-cone projections. Formulas containing \(1/\alpha\), \(1/(1-\alpha)\), or unscaled logarithms are numerically ill-conditioned near these endpoints and should be replaced by limit-aware branches.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: As the exponent reaches an endpoint, the power cone becomes a nonnegative coordinate times a two-dimensional second-order cone; ordinary formulas become ill-conditioned.
assumptions_latex: The limits are understood as convergence of closed convex cones.
Projection inputs remain fixed while \(\alpha\) approaches an endpoint.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Pi_{K_\alpha}(q)\to\Pi_{K_0}(q)\) as \(\alpha\downarrow0\), and \(\Pi_{K_\alpha}(q)\to\Pi_{K_1}(q)\) as \(\alpha\uparrow1\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind fits the container, but the mode of closed-cone convergence, consequent projection convergence, and numerical-conditioning recommendation require a specific source.

knowledge_statements.title: Relative-Entropy-Cone Projection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: KKT projection mechanism for the scalar relative-entropy cone, including boundary checks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define \(K_{\mathrm{re}}=\operatorname{cl}\{(t,x,y):x>0,\ y>0,\ x\log(x/y)\le t\}\). For input \((a,b,c)\), first apply membership and polar tests. A smooth-boundary candidate satisfies, for some \(\lambda>0\),
\[t=a+\lambda,\quad x-b+\lambda(\log(x/y)+1)=0,\quad y-c-\lambda x/y=0,\quad x\log(x/y)=t.\]
Solve these equations with \(x,y>0\), compare the result with projections onto the closure's lower-dimensional faces, and return the feasible candidate minimizing Euclidean distance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Relative-entropy-cone projection uses membership tests, a smooth KKT system, and explicit comparison with closure-face candidates.
assumptions_latex: The closed perspective convention defines \(K_{\mathrm{re}}\).
The nonlinear equations are solved over \(x>0\) and \(y>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The least-distance feasible candidate equals \(\Pi_{K_{\mathrm{re}}}(a,b,c)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The smooth KKT equations are plausible and fit an algorithm record, but the closure-face candidates are not identified and the completeness of the projection mechanism is unsupported.

knowledge_statements.title: Sparse Quasidefinite Factorization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pivot-free signed factorization of regularized sparse quasidefinite affine-solve systems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let
\[Q=\begin{pmatrix}P&A^{\mathsf T}\\A&-D\end{pmatrix},\]
where \(P\in\mathbb S_{++}^n\), \(D\in\mathbb S_{++}^m\), and \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\). Then \(Q\) is symmetric quasidefinite and nonsingular. Under any symmetric permutation, it admits an \(LDL^{\mathsf T}\) factorization without dynamic numerical pivoting; the diagonal pivots have \(n\) positive and \(m\) negative signs. A fill-reducing permutation may therefore be selected symbolically from the sparsity pattern and used for the numeric factorization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A regularized saddle-point matrix with positive and negative definite diagonal blocks has a stable-sign LDLᵀ structure compatible with sparse symbolic ordering.
assumptions_latex: \(P\succ0\) and \(D\succ0\)
The same symmetric permutation is applied to rows and columns.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Q\) is nonsingular and possesses a pivot-free signed \(LDL^{\mathsf T}\) factorization.

notation.meaning: positive definite lower diagonal block; the factor diagonal is distinguished by context

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property fits the sparse-factorization container, but the strong claims about every symmetric permutation, pivot-free factorization, and pivot signs require a theorem-level source. Using D for both the matrix block and factor diagonal is also ambiguous.

knowledge_statements.title: Symbolic Factorization Reuse
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reuses ordering and elimination structure while matrix values change but sparsity remains fixed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q_k\) be symmetric matrices having one fixed sparsity pattern and a fixed pivot-free factorization structure. Once, compute a symmetric fill-reducing permutation \(\Pi\), the elimination tree, and the nonzero pattern of \(L\) for \(\Pi Q_k\Pi^{\mathsf T}=L_kD_kL_k^{\mathsf T}\). For each new numerical instance, retain these symbolic objects and recompute only \(L_k\) and \(D_k\). Rebuild the symbolic factorization whenever the sparsity pattern, block dimensions, permutation, or admissible pivot structure changes.

assumptions_latex: All reused matrices have identical structural nonzeros and dimensions.

knowledge_statements.title: Refactorization Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Validity boundary for reuse of factors in a direct affine-solve oracle.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the stored factors represent a nonsingular matrix \(K_0\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\). They may be reused for a current direct solve \(Kx=b\) only when they still represent \(K\), either because \(K=K_0\) or because a validated update procedure has transformed the factors to represent \(K\). If \(K\neq K_0\) and no such update is applied, or if changed pivoting or regularization changes the represented operator, the stored factors are invalid for that direct solve and a new factorization is required. For a computed solution \(\widehat{x}\), define \(d=\lVert K\rVert\lVert\widehat{x}\rVert+\lVert b\rVert\). When \(d>0\), a backward-error ratio \(\lVert b-K\widehat{x}\rVert/d\) above a prescribed tolerance triggers the solver's corrective policy, which may include refinement, a validated update, or refactorization; when \(d=0\), the residual is zero and the ratio is taken to be zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Stored factors remain valid only while they represent the current operator, directly or through a validated update. An excessive backward error triggers corrective action, with refactorization required when the current operator is not represented and no valid update is available.
assumptions_latex: The stored factors represent a nonsingular matrix \(K_0\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\).

knowledge_statements.title: Partial-Orthogonality Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Block elimination induced by a row-orthonormal subset of constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) be partitioned by rows as \(A=[A_1;A_2]\), where \(A_1\in\mathbb{R}^{k\times n}\), \(A_2\in\mathbb{R}^{(m-k)\times n}\), and \(A_1A_1^{\mathsf T}=I_k\). Then \[I_m+AA^{\mathsf T}=\begin{bmatrix}2I_k&A_1A_2^{\mathsf T}\\A_2A_1^{\mathsf T}&I_{m-k}+A_2A_2^{\mathsf T}\end{bmatrix}.\] Eliminating the first block uses \((2I_k)^{-1}=\tfrac12 I_k\) and the Schur complement \[S=I_{m-k}+A_2A_2^{\mathsf T}-\tfrac12 A_2A_1^{\mathsf T}A_1A_2^{\mathsf T}.\] If \(S\) is nonsingular, applying \((I_m+AA^{\mathsf T})^{-1}\) reduces to one solve with \(S\), multiplication by the cross blocks, and application of \(\tfrac12 I_k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A row-orthonormal block gives an explicit leading-block inverse, while the remaining part of the normal-system solve is a Schur-complement solve containing the required one-half factor.

The rows of \(A_1\) are orthonormal, so \(A_1A_1^{\mathsf T}=I_k\).
The matrix \(S=I_{m-k}+A_2A_2^{\mathsf T}-\tfrac12 A_2A_1^{\mathsf T}A_1A_2^{\mathsf T}\) is nonsingular.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The projection and multiplier are the unique solution of \[\begin{bmatrix}I&A^{\mathsf T}\\A&0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x\\y\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}z\\b\end{bmatrix}.\] Eliminating \(x=z-A^{\mathsf T}y\) gives the Schur-complement system \[(AA^{\mathsf T})y=Az-b,\] after which \(x=z-A^{\mathsf T}y\). assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) has no zero columns.
The Euclidean column norm is used.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The scaled matrix \(AD_c\) has unit Euclidean norm in every column.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One Euclidean column-normalization step with consistent variable scaling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) with \(\|A_{:j}\|_2>0\) for every \(j\), define \[D_c=\operatorname{diag}\bigl(\|A_{:1}\|_2^{-1},\ldots,\|A_{:n}\|_2^{-1}\bigr).\] Replace \(A\) by \(AD_c\) and reparameterize the primal variable by \(x=D_c\widetilde x\); transform objective coefficients and cone coordinates consistently. Then \(\|(AD_c)_{:j}\|_2=1\) for every column. Zero columns require separate treatment rather than reciprocal scaling.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Scale every nonzero matrix column by its reciprocal norm and transform variables and objective data consistently.
knowledge_statements.title: Column Equilibration

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits and reciprocal column scaling produces unit column norms, but the cited norms section does not support the equilibration algorithm or the asserted consistent transformations of variables, objectives, and cone coordinates.

children.title: Alternating Row–Column Equilibration
children.top_down_role: Coupled equilibration regimes alternating between constraint-side and variable-side scaling.

knowledge_statements.title: Alternating Row–Column Equilibration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Alternating diagonal normalization for the linear map in a finite-dimensional conic formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), tolerance \(\varepsilon>0\), and positive floor \(\delta\), initialize \(D_0=I_m\) and \(E_0=I_n\). At cycle \(k\), set \(B_k=D_kAE_k\), choose positive row factors \(r_i=(\max\{\lVert (B_k)_{i,:}\rVert_2,\delta\})^{-1}\), and update \(D_{k+1}=\operatorname{diag}(r)D_k\). Next set \(C_k=D_{k+1}AE_k\), choose \(q_j=(\max\{\lVert (C_k)_{:,j}\rVert_2,\delta\})^{-1}\), and update \(E_{k+1}=E_k\operatorname{diag}(q)\). Stop when every nonzero row and column norm of \(D_{k+1}AE_{k+1}\) lies in \([1-\varepsilon,1+\varepsilon]\), or when a prescribed cycle limit is reached; output \((D_{k+1},E_{k+1})\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Alternately normalize rows and columns of the scaled constraint matrix until their nonzero norms are near one or the cycle limit is reached.
assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\)
\(\varepsilon>0\) and \(\delta>0\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output is a pair of positive diagonal matrices \((D,E)\) defining the equilibrated map \(DAE\).

notation.meaning: cumulative row and column scaling matrices
floor preventing division by zero or very small norms

review_flags: No supplied source locator directly supports this alternating equilibration algorithm.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits the terminal container, and the variables and stopping rule are explicit. However, no citation or inspectable locator supports this particular alternating Euclidean row-column normalization, floor convention, or stopping criterion. The supplied inventory does not address matrix equilibration, so source uncertainty is material.

knowledge_statements.title: Cone-Preserving Scaling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scaling transformations that leave the slack cone invariant.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a closed convex cone \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^m\), a cone-preserving scaling is an invertible linear map \(S:\mathbb{R}^m\to\mathbb{R}^m\) satisfying \(S(K)=K\). Applied to the conic constraint \(Ax+s=b\) with \(s\in K\), it produces \(SAx+s'=Sb\), where \(s'=Ss\in K\). Conversely, every feasible \((x,s')\) of the scaled constraint corresponds to the original slack \(s=S^{-1}s'\in K\). Thus the scaling changes the numerical representation without changing primal feasibility or the objective function.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An invertible scaling preserves a cone when it maps that cone onto itself; applying it to a conic equality preserves feasibility bijectively.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^m\) is a closed convex cone
\(S\) is invertible and \(S(K)=K\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Ax+s=b,\ s\in K\iff SAx+Ss=Sb,\ Ss\in K\).

notation.meaning: invertible cone automorphism used for scaling

review_flags: Supplied cone references do not directly document solver-data scaling by cone automorphisms.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition kind fits Cone-Preserving Scaling, and the stated feasibility correspondence is mathematically coherent for an invertible map satisfying S(K)=K. No cited source with a specific locator supports its use as conic solver-data scaling, and the inventory's general cone references are not sufficient evidence for this claim.

children.title: Objective Scale Balancing
children.top_down_role: Scaling choices governing the numerical magnitude of objective data.

knowledge_statements.title: Objective Scale Balancing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive normalization of the objective coefficients relative to a selected target magnitude.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the conic program with objective \(c^{\mathsf T}x\), choose a target magnitude \(t>0\), a floor \(\delta>0\), and a coefficient norm \(\lVert\cdot\rVert\). Set \(\gamma=t/\max\{\lVert c\rVert,\delta\}\) and replace \(c\) by \(\widehat c=\gamma c\). Solve the resulting problem using objective value \(\widehat c^{\mathsf T}x\), and recover the original reported objective by \(c^{\mathsf T}x=\gamma^{-1}\widehat c^{\mathsf T}x\). Because \(\gamma>0\), the feasible set and ordering of feasible objective values are unchanged, so the primal minimizers are identical.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Multiply objective coefficients by a positive factor that gives them a target norm, then undo that factor when reporting objective values.
assumptions_latex: The feasible set is unchanged by objective scaling
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in F}c^{\mathsf T}x=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in F}(\gamma c)^{\mathsf T}x\) for \(\gamma>0\).
review_flags: No supplied locator supports this particular objective normalization convention.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind is appropriate for Objective Scale Balancing, and positive objective scaling preserves minimizers. The target-norm formula, floor convention, and solver reporting prescription are uncited implementation choices. No supplied locator supports this exact balancing algorithm.

children.title: Constraint Scale Balancing
children.top_down_role: Scaling choices governing the numerical magnitude of constraint data.

knowledge_statements.title: Constraint Scale Balancing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Row scaling that balances affine conic constraints while preserving their solution correspondence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(Ax+s=b\) with \(s\in K\), choose a norm \(\lVert\cdot\rVert\), floor \(\delta>0\), and positive diagonal \(D=\operatorname{diag}(d_1,\ldots,d_m)\), where \(d_i=(\max\{\lVert(A_{i,:},b_i)\rVert,\delta\})^{-1}\). If \(D(K)=K\), replace the constraint by \(DAx+\widehat s=Db\), with \(\widehat s=Ds\in K\). Each nonzero augmented row \((DA_{i,:},(Db)_i)\) then has unit norm unless the floor is active. Recover the original slack as \(s=D^{-1}\widehat s\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Scale each affine constraint row to controlled magnitude, requiring the diagonal map to preserve the slack cone so feasibility remains equivalent.
assumptions_latex: \(Ax+s=b\) and \(s\in K\)
\(D\) is positive diagonal and satisfies \(D(K)=K\)
\(\delta>0\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Ax+s=b,\ s\in K\iff DAx+Ds=Db,\ Ds\in K\).
review_flags: No supplied locator directly supports the stated row-balancing convention and cone restriction.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits the container, and requiring D(K)=K gives the stated feasibility correspondence. Nevertheless, the augmented-row norm convention and the restriction to cone-preserving diagonal scalings require direct support. None of the supplied sources addresses this solver equilibration procedure.

children.title: Objective–Constraint Scale Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Numerical tradeoffs between objective normalization and constraint normalization.

knowledge_statements.title: Objective–Constraint Scale Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Effect of equivalent data scaling on solver residuals, gaps, and termination tests.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a conic problem whose objective is multiplied by \(\gamma>0\) and whose equality constraints are transformed by an invertible cone-preserving map \(D\). Exact primal solutions correspond bijectively under the scaling, but an unscaled objective gap is multiplied by \(\gamma\), while the equality residual becomes \(D(Ax+s-b)\). Consequently, absolute stopping tests in scaled coordinates generally represent different original-coordinate accuracies. Objective and constraint scales should therefore be selected jointly, and termination diagnostics should be mapped back or normalized by compatible scale factors before accuracy is interpreted.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Equivalent scaling preserves exact solutions but changes numerical gaps and residual norms, so objective and constraint scales must be coordinated with stopping tests.
assumptions_latex: \(\gamma>0\)
\(D\) is invertible and cone-preserving
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat g=\gamma g\) and \(\widehat r_p=Dr_p\), so fixed absolute thresholds are not invariant under scaling.
review_flags: The supplied references do not directly support residual and gap transformations for first-order solver diagnostics.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The principle kind correctly matches a tradeoff container. The residual transformation is coherent, but the meaning of the objective-gap quantity depends on the primal-dual formulation and on how dual variables are rescaled. No source defines those diagnostics or supports the joint interpretation of scaled stopping tolerances.

knowledge_statements.title: Diagonal-Metric Preconditioning
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Variable-metric primal–dual splitting with positive diagonal metrics.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the saddle problem \(\min_x\max_y f(x)+\langle Kx,y\rangle-g^*(y)\), diagonal-metric preconditioning selects positive diagonal matrices \(T\) and \(\Sigma\) and uses the updates \(x^{k+1}=\operatorname{prox}^{T^{-1}}_f(x^k-TK^{\mathsf T}y^k)\) and \(y^{k+1}=\operatorname{prox}^{\Sigma^{-1}}_{g^*}(y^k+\Sigma K\bar x^{k+1})\). Here \(\operatorname{prox}^{M}_h(v)=\operatorname*{argmin}_u\{h(u)+\tfrac12\lVert u-v\rVert_M^2\}\). A standard compatibility condition is \(\lVert\Sigma^{1/2}KT^{1/2}\rVert_2<1\); diagonal entries act as coordinatewise step sizes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive diagonal primal and dual metrics provide coordinatewise step sizes, subject to a scaled-operator norm condition.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) and \(g^*\) are proper, closed, and convex
\(T\succ0\) and \(\Sigma\succ0\) are diagonal
\(\lVert\Sigma^{1/2}KT^{1/2}\rVert_2<1\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The iteration is a primal–dual proximal splitting performed in the diagonal metrics \(T^{-1}\) and \(\Sigma^{-1}\).

notation.meaning: diagonal primal and dual step-size matrices

review_flags: No supplied locator supports this variable-metric primal–dual splitting formulation.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: A definition is a plausible kind for the topic, but the record embeds a specific primal-dual algorithm and compatibility condition rather than only defining diagonal-metric preconditioning. The extrapolated point bar x^{k+1} is not introduced, and no locator supports the stated update convention or convergence-compatible norm bound.

knowledge_statements.title: Block-Metric Preconditioning
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primal–dual preconditioning using positive-definite metrics aligned with variable blocks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Partition the primal and dual spaces into blocks and consider \(\min_x\max_y f(x)+\langle Kx,y\rangle-g^*(y)\). Block-metric preconditioning chooses \(T=\operatorname{blkdiag}(T_1,\ldots,T_p)\succ0\) and \(\Sigma=\operatorname{blkdiag}(\Sigma_1,\ldots,\Sigma_q)\succ0\). The associated proximal steps use the metrics \(T^{-1}\) and \(\Sigma^{-1}\), allowing coupled scaling within each block. The preconditioner is compatible with the linear coupling when \(\lVert\Sigma^{1/2}KT^{1/2}\rVert_2<1\). Scalar and diagonal step sizes are recovered when every block is respectively scalar or diagonal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Block-metric preconditioning assigns a positive-definite step metric to each primal and dual block while controlling the scaled coupling operator.
assumptions_latex: The primal and dual spaces have fixed finite block decompositions
\(T_i\succ0\) and \(\Sigma_j\succ0\)
\(\lVert\Sigma^{1/2}KT^{1/2}\rVert_2<1\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T\) and \(\Sigma\) define blockwise proximal metrics compatible with \(K\).

notation.meaning: positive-definite metric on primal block i
positive-definite metric on dual block j

review_flags: No supplied locator supports block-metric first-order primal–dual preconditioning.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition kind fits the topic, and the distinction between block and diagonal metrics is clear. However, the claimed operator-norm compatibility condition belongs to a particular primal-dual splitting formulation and is unsupported by any supplied citation. The source inventory does not cover block-metric preconditioning.

knowledge_statements.title: Adaptive Primal–Dual Scaling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Residual-driven adaptation of reciprocal primal and dual step sizes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(\tau_0>0\), \(\sigma_0>0\), adaptation factor \(\eta>1\), and balance threshold \(\mu>1\), with \(\tau_0\sigma_0\lVert K\rVert_2^2<1\). After iteration \(k\), compute nonnegative primal and dual residual measures \(p_k\) and \(d_k\). If \(p_k>\mu d_k\), set \((\tau_{k+1},\sigma_{k+1})=(\tau_k/\eta,\eta\sigma_k)\); if \(d_k>\mu p_k\), set \((\tau_{k+1},\sigma_{k+1})=(\eta\tau_k,\sigma_k/\eta)\); otherwise retain both steps. Use the new pair in the next primal–dual update and stop under the solver's residual criteria.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adapt reciprocal primal and dual step sizes according to residual imbalance while preserving their product and the initial stability bound.
assumptions_latex: \(\tau_0\sigma_0\lVert K\rVert_2^2<1\)
\(p_k,d_k\ge0\) use compatible normalization
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\tau_{k+1}\sigma_{k+1}=\tau_k\sigma_k\), while the step-size ratio responds to primal–dual residual imbalance.

notation.meaning: normalized primal and dual residual measures

review_flags: Residual definitions and convergence safeguards vary by solver; no directly relevant source locator was supplied.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits Adaptive Primal-Dual Scaling, but p_k and d_k are only described generically, so the comparisons do not define a reproducible solver algorithm. Preserving the step-size product preserves the initial scalar bound, but whether the adaptation is valid depends on the underlying splitting method and residual definitions. No supporting locator is supplied.

knowledge_statements.title: Under-Relaxation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Krasnosel'skii–Mann update with a relaxation parameter below one.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a fixed-point operator \(T:H\to H\), an initial point \(z^0\in H\), and \(\alpha\in(0,1)\), compute \(u^k=Tz^k\) and \(z^{k+1}=(1-\alpha)z^k+\alpha u^k\). Stop when \(\lVert u^k-z^k\rVert\le\varepsilon\) or an iteration limit is reached, and output \(z^k\). Each update lies strictly between the current point and the full operator step. If \(T\) is nonexpansive and has a fixed point, standard Krasnosel'skii–Mann conditions yield asymptotic regularity and weak convergence in Hilbert space for constant \(\alpha\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under-relaxation moves only a fraction between the current iterate and the full fixed-point update, using a parameter strictly between zero and one.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a Hilbert space
\(T:H\to H\) is nonexpansive with \(\operatorname{Fix}T\ne\varnothing\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(z^{k+1}=(1-\alpha)z^k+\alpha Tz^k\), with \(\lVert Tz^k-z^k\rVert\to0\).

notation.meaning: fixed-point operator induced by the splitting method

review_flags: No supplied source locator supports the Krasnosel'skii–Mann convergence statement.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits Under-Relaxation, and the Krasnoselskii-Mann update is stated consistently. The appended asymptotic-regularity and weak-convergence theorem is nontrivial and has no citation or locator. None of the inventory sources supports fixed-point relaxation theory.

knowledge_statements.title: Over-Relaxation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relaxed fixed-point iteration beyond the full step for firmly nonexpansive operators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T:H\to H\) be firmly nonexpansive with \(\operatorname{Fix}T\ne\varnothing\). For a constant relaxation parameter \(\alpha\in(1,2)\), define \(z^{k+1}=z^k+\alpha(Tz^k-z^k)\). The relaxed mapping \(R_\alpha=(1-\alpha)I+\alpha T\) remains averaged, although \(z^{k+1}\) extrapolates beyond \(Tz^k\) along the line from \(z^k\) to \(Tz^k\). The iterates converge weakly to a fixed point of \(T\), and the fixed-point residual \(\lVert Tz^k-z^k\rVert\) tends to zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a firmly nonexpansive operator, relaxation between one and two extrapolates beyond the full step while retaining averagedness and fixed-point convergence.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a Hilbert space
\(T\) is firmly nonexpansive and \(\operatorname{Fix}T\ne\varnothing\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R_\alpha=(1-\alpha)I+\alpha T\) is averaged and \(z^k\rightharpoonup z^\star\in\operatorname{Fix}T\).
review_flags: No supplied source locator supports this firmly nonexpansive over-relaxation result.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property kind is defensible because the record primarily states averagedness and convergence of the relaxed mapping, although it also supplies an iteration rule. The firmly nonexpansive over-relaxation theorem is mathematically specific and nontrivial, and no inspectable source locator supports it.

knowledge_statements.title: Adaptive Relaxation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Iteration-dependent relaxation with safeguards for a firmly nonexpansive fixed-point map.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a firmly nonexpansive map \(T:H\to H\), choose safeguards \(0<\underline\alpha\le\overline\alpha<2\), an initial point \(z^0\), and tolerance \(\varepsilon>0\). At iteration \(k\), select \(\alpha_k\in[\underline\alpha,\overline\alpha]\) from available residual or progress diagnostics, then set \(z^{k+1}=z^k+\alpha_k(Tz^k-z^k)\). Accept only parameters within the safeguards, regardless of the adaptation rule. Stop when \(\lVert Tz^k-z^k\rVert\le\varepsilon\). If \(\operatorname{Fix}T\ne\varnothing\), the safeguarded sequence satisfies the standard variable-relaxation convergence condition \(\sum_k\alpha_k(2-\alpha_k)=\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose relaxation parameters from diagnostics but keep them bounded away from zero and two; these safeguards retain the standard convergence condition.
assumptions_latex: \(T\) is firmly nonexpansive with \(\operatorname{Fix}T\ne\varnothing\)
\(0<\underline\alpha\le\alpha_k\le\overline\alpha<2\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(z^{k+1}=z^k+\alpha_k(Tz^k-z^k)\) and \(\sum_k\alpha_k(2-\alpha_k)=\infty\).
review_flags: The diagnostic selection rule is intentionally generic, and no directly relevant source locator was supplied.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits the container, but selecting alpha_k from unspecified diagnostics does not define a reproducible adaptive rule. The safeguards do imply divergence of the displayed sum, yet convergence of the resulting variable-relaxation iteration is a nontrivial sourced result. No relevant locator is supplied.

knowledge_statements.title: Inertial Splitting Variants
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic extrapolated fixed-point template underlying inertial first-order splitting variants.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T:H\to H\) denote one full step of a fixed-point splitting method. Initialize \(z^{-1}=z^0\), choose inertial parameters \(\beta_k\ge0\) and relaxation parameters \(\alpha_k>0\), and form \(w^k=z^k+\beta_k(z^k-z^{k-1})\). Compute \(u^k=Tw^k\) and update \(z^{k+1}=w^k+\alpha_k(u^k-w^k)\). Stop when a prescribed fixed-point or primal–dual residual at \(w^k\) is below tolerance. The noninertial method is recovered by \(\beta_k=0\); convergence requires method-specific bounds coupling \(\beta_k\), \(\alpha_k\), and the averagedness of \(T\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An inertial splitting method extrapolates from the last two iterates before applying a relaxed fixed-point step; stability bounds depend on the underlying operator.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a Hilbert space
\(T:H\to H\) is the fixed-point map of the chosen splitting method
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(w^k=z^k+\beta_k(z^k-z^{k-1})\) and \(z^{k+1}=w^k+\alpha_k(Tw^k-w^k)\).
review_flags: Convergence restrictions are splitting-specific, and no supplied locator identifies a particular inertial variant.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind is suitable for a generic inertial template, and the formulas are internally consistent. However, the terminal title concerns splitting variants while the record identifies no particular splitting method and gives no usable stability or convergence conditions. Those conditions are explicitly method-specific, and no source locator supports the template or its scope.

knowledge_statements.title: Type-I Anderson Acceleration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Multisecant Jacobian form for accelerating a fixed-point residual equation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(T:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(F(x)=x-T(x)\). At iteration \(k\), retain differences \(\Delta X_k=[x_{i+1}-x_i]\) and \(\Delta F_k=[F(x_{i+1})-F(x_i)]\). Type-I Anderson acceleration computes
\[B_k\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{B}\|B-I\|_F^2\quad\text{subject to}\quad B\Delta X_k=\Delta F_k,\]
and, when the selected \(B_k\) is nonsingular, sets \(x_{k+1}=x_k-B_k^{-1}F(x_k)\). With empty history, \(B_k=I\), so the update reduces to \(x_{k+1}=T(x_k)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Type-I acceleration fits a residual Jacobian satisfying recent secant equations and applies its inverse to the current fixed-point residual.
assumptions_latex: \(T:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\) is evaluable at every accepted iterate.
The multisecant constraints are consistent.
The selected \(B_k\) is nonsingular.
review_flags: Exact Type-I convention and multisecant formulation require an authoritative Anderson-acceleration source.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm role fits the Type-I leaf, and the variables and update are internally coherent. However, no citation is supplied for the naming convention, Frobenius-minimal multisecant Jacobian formula, consistency assumptions, or nonsingular-selection rule; these conventions vary across Anderson-acceleration sources.

knowledge_statements.title: Type-II Anderson Acceleration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Multisecant inverse-Jacobian form for accelerating a fixed-point residual equation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(T:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(F(x)=x-T(x)\). From retained differences \(\Delta X_k\) and \(\Delta F_k\), Type-II Anderson acceleration computes
\[H_k\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{H}\|H-I\|_F^2\quad\text{subject to}\quad H\Delta F_k=\Delta X_k,\]
and updates \(x_{k+1}=x_k-H_kF(x_k)\). When the history is empty, \(H_k=I\) and the update is the underlying fixed-point step \(x_{k+1}=T(x_k)\). Rank-deficient histories require column removal, a pseudoinverse convention, or regularization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Type-II acceleration fits an inverse residual Jacobian satisfying recent inverse-secant equations and applies it directly to the current residual.
assumptions_latex: \(T:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\) is evaluable at every accepted iterate.
The inverse-multisecant constraints are consistent.
review_flags: Exact Type-II convention and inverse-multisecant formulation require an authoritative Anderson-acceleration source.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm role fits the Type-II leaf, and the inverse-multisecant update is coherent. An authoritative source with a specific locator is required to verify the Type-II naming convention, constrained Frobenius formulation, and treatment of rank-deficient history.

knowledge_statements.title: Regularized Anderson Acceleration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tikhonov-regularized inverse-multisecant acceleration for ill-conditioned histories.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F(x)=x-T(x)\), choose \(\lambda_k>0\), and form history matrices \(\Delta X_k\) and \(\Delta F_k\). Compute the unique regularized approximation
\[H_k=\operatorname*{argmin}_{H}\left\{\|H-I\|_F^2+\lambda_k^{-1}\|H\Delta F_k-\Delta X_k\|_F^2\right\},\]
then propose \(x_{k+1}=x_k-H_kF(x_k)\). Positive regularization makes the fitting problem strongly convex even when \(\Delta F_k\) is rank deficient. Increasing \(\lambda_k\) pulls \(H_k\) toward \(I\), while decreasing it emphasizes the multisecant fit.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Regularized Anderson acceleration stabilizes an ill-conditioned multisecant fit by penalizing deviation from the baseline inverse Jacobian.
assumptions_latex: \(T:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\) is evaluable.
\(\lambda_k>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_{k+1}=x_k-H_kF(x_k)\), with a uniquely defined \(H_k\).
review_flags: The intended regularization convention may instead regularize Anderson mixing coefficients; a source is needed to select the canonical local version.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm role fits the regularized-acceleration leaf, and the stated objective is strongly convex because of the squared distance to the identity. No source establishes that this inverse-Jacobian penalty, its lambda scaling, and the resulting update are the intended regularized Anderson variant rather than coefficient regularization or another convention.

knowledge_statements.title: Safeguarded Anderson Acceleration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Residual-based acceptance wrapper preserving a reliable baseline fixed-point step.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given \(x_k\), form a baseline candidate \(b_k=T(x_k)\) and an Anderson candidate \(a_k\). Choose parameters \(0<\eta<1\) and \(M\geq1\). Accept
\[x_{k+1}=a_k\quad\text{if}\quad \|F(a_k)\|\leq\eta\|F(x_k)\|\quad\text{and}\quad \|a_k-x_k\|\leq M\|b_k-x_k\|;\]
otherwise set \(x_{k+1}=b_k\) and optionally clear the Anderson history. Thus every rejected accelerated proposal is replaced by the underlying fixed-point update, while accepted proposals satisfy explicit residual and step-size tests.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A safeguard accepts an Anderson proposal only after residual and step tests; otherwise it executes the baseline fixed-point step.
assumptions_latex: \(F(x)=x-T(x)\) can be evaluated at each candidate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_{k+1}\in\{a_k,b_k\}\), and \(a_k\) is chosen only when both safeguard inequalities hold.
review_flags: Safeguard tests vary across conic solvers; an implementation or convergence source is needed for the intended regime.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm role fits the safeguarded-acceleration leaf, and the acceptance wrapper is precisely stated. The particular residual contraction and relative step-size tests are not canonical across Anderson or conic-splitting implementations, so a source with a specific algorithm or section locator is needed.

knowledge_statements.title: Solution Warm Starts
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Initialization of a related conic solve from a previously computed solution state.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider related conic problems \(P(\theta_j)\) solved by an iteration with state \(z=(x,y,s,\tau,\kappa)\). After obtaining an approximate solution \(z_{j-1}\) for \(P(\theta_{j-1})\), choose an admissibility map \(\Pi_j\) for the new problem and initialize
\[z_j^0=\Pi_j(z_{j-1}).\]
The map must enforce the solver's domain requirements, such as projecting cone-valued components into the required cones and resetting invalid scaling variables. The solver then applies its ordinary stopping tests to \(P(\theta_j)\); warm starting changes initialization, not the requested accuracy or certificate conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A warm start maps a prior primal-dual solution state into an admissible initial state for a related conic problem.
assumptions_latex: Successive problems share compatible variable and cone representations.
\(\Pi_j(z_{j-1})\) lies in the new solver state's admissible domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(z_j^0=\Pi_j(z_{j-1})\) initializes the solve of \(P(\theta_j)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Factorization Caching
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reuse of symbolic or numeric linear-system factorizations across compatible solves.

knowledge_statements.title: Cache Invalidation Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditions requiring complete or partial invalidation of cached solver artifacts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a cache entry be \(C=(K_s,K_n,A)\), where \(K_s\) encodes structure, \(K_n\) encodes numerical values and settings, and \(A\) is the cached artifact. A structural-key change invalidates the entire entry. If \(K_s\) is unchanged but \(K_n\) changes, numerical artifacts are invalidated while compatible allocations and symbolic analyses may remain. No invalidation is required only when both keys match and the artifact has not been externally mutated. Any failed integrity or residual check forces invalidation regardless of key equality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Structural changes invalidate everything; numerical changes invalidate numeric artifacts; integrity failures invalidate the affected cache regardless of key matches.
assumptions_latex: The keys cover every dependency of the cached artifact.
Cache integrity and residual checks are available where applicable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K_s'\neq K_s\) implies full invalidation, while \(K_s'=K_s\) and \(K_n'\neq K_n\) imply numerical invalidation.
review_flags: The precise invalidation dependencies are implementation-specific and need solver documentation.

knowledge_statements.title: Parameter Continuation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential solution along a parameter path using adaptive warm starts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P(\theta)\) be a parameterized conic problem and choose a path \(\theta_0,\ldots,\theta_N\). Solve \(P(\theta_0)\) to the prescribed tolerance. For \(j=1,\ldots,N\), map the preceding state into an admissible warm start for \(P(\theta_j)\), solve, and record its stopping certificate. If the solve fails or exceeds a prescribed effort limit, insert intermediate parameter values between \(\theta_{j-1}\) and \(\theta_j\) and retry. Output the certified state at \(\theta_N\); intermediate warm starts do not replace final feasibility or accuracy tests.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Continuation traverses a parameter path, warm-starting each conic solve and refining the path when a step is too difficult.
assumptions_latex: Each \(P(\theta_j)\) has a compatible conic representation.
A map produces admissible warm starts between consecutive problems.
Every accepted solve satisfies the prescribed stopping tests.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The algorithm returns a solver-certified state for \(P(\theta_N)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Fejér Monotonicity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Metric monotonicity of an iterate sequence relative to a target set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H\) be a Hilbert space and let \(C\subseteq H\) be nonempty. A sequence \((x_k)_{k\geq0}\subseteq H\) is Fejér monotone with respect to \(C\) if
\[\|x_{k+1}-c\|\leq\|x_k-c\|\qquad\text{for every }c\in C\text{ and every }k\geq0.\]
Consequently, for each \(c\in C\), the scalar sequence \((\|x_k-c\|)_{k\geq0}\) is nonincreasing and convergent, and \((x_k)_{k\geq0}\) is bounded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A sequence is Fejér monotone when its distance to every point of a nonempty target set never increases.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a Hilbert space.
\(C\subseteq H\) is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\|x_{k+1}-c\|\leq\|x_k-c\|\) for all \(c\in C\) and \(k\geq0\).

knowledge_statements.title: Averaged-Operator Convergence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weak convergence of Picard iteration for an averaged mapping on a Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space, let \(T:H\to H\) be \(\alpha\)-averaged for some \(0<\alpha<1\), and suppose \(\operatorname{Fix}T\neq\varnothing\). For any \(x_0\in H\), define \(x_{k+1}=Tx_k\). Then \((x_k)\) converges weakly to some \(x_\star\in\operatorname{Fix}T\), and \(\|x_k-Tx_k\|\to0\). If \(H\) is finite-dimensional, the convergence is in norm. Here averagedness means \(T=(1-\alpha)I+\alpha R\) for a nonexpansive mapping \(R:H\to H\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Picard iteration of an averaged operator with a fixed point converges weakly to a fixed point and its residual vanishes.

knowledge_statements.title: Asymptotic Regularization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Vanishing successive-step or fixed-point residual behavior of an iterative sequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A sequence \((x_k)_{k\geq0}\) in a normed space is asymptotically regular if
\[\|x_{k+1}-x_k\|\longrightarrow0.\]
For a Picard iteration \(x_{k+1}=Tx_k\), this condition is equivalent to \(\|Tx_k-x_k\|\to0\). An operator \(T\) is asymptotically regular at \(x_0\) when its orbit \((T^kx_0)_{k\geq0}\) has this property, and it is asymptotically regular when this holds for every initial point in its domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Asymptotic regularity means consecutive iterates approach one another; for fixed-point iteration, this is exactly vanishing fixed-point residual.
assumptions_latex: The iterates lie in a normed space.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the saddle problem \(\min_x\max_y f(x)+\langle Kx,y\rangle-g^*(y)\), with proper closed convex \(f\) and \(g^*\), scalar-step PDHG uses \(\tau>0\) and \(\sigma>0\). Its standard positive-definite metric condition is \[\tau\sigma\lVert K\rVert^2<1.\] Equivalently, the block operator \(H=\begin{pmatrix}\tau^{-1}I&-K^*\\-K&\sigma^{-1}I\end{pmatrix}\) is positive definite. Under this condition and existence of a saddle point, the usual fixed-step convergence and ergodic-gap estimates apply.

Define \(\bar x_N=N^{-1}\sum_{k=1}^N x^k\) and \(\bar y_N=N^{-1}\sum_{k=1}^N y^k\). Then for every comparison pair \((x,y)\), \[\mathcal L(\bar x_N,y)-\mathcal L(x,\bar y_N)\le\frac{\lVert(x,y)-(x^0,y^0)\rVert_H^2}{2N}.\] Taking the supremum over any bounded test set gives an \(O(1/N)\) restricted primal--dual-gap bound and therefore \(O(1/\varepsilon)\) iterations for gap tolerance \(\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Averaged PDHG iterates have restricted primal--dual gap at most an initial metric-distance constant divided by the iteration count.
knowledge_statements.title: Ergodic Primal–Dual-Gap Rates

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Complexity_bound fits the leaf, but the exact constant, metric, averaging indices, and applicability to every comparison pair depend on the PDHG convention and require a specifically located source.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Best-iterate fixed-point residual for firmly nonexpansive splitting.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T:H\to H\) be firmly nonexpansive, let \(F=\operatorname{Fix}T\neq\varnothing\), and define \(z^{k+1}=Tz^k\) and \(R_k=\lVert z^k-Tz^k\rVert\). Firm nonexpansiveness implies, for every \(z^\star\in F\), \[\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}R_k^2\le\lVert z^0-z^\star\rVert^2.\] Minimizing over \(z^\star\in F\) and then over the first \(N\) residuals yields \[\min_{0\le k<N}R_k\le\frac{\operatorname{dist}(z^0,F)}{\sqrt N}.\] Thus an iterate with residual at most \(\varepsilon\) is guaranteed within \(O(1/\varepsilon^2)\) operator evaluations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Among the first N firmly nonexpansive iterates, one fixed-point residual is at most the initial fixed-point distance divided by the square root of N.
knowledge_statements.title: Best-Iterate Residual Rates

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The best-iterate residual estimate is mathematically standard for firmly nonexpansive mappings and complexity_bound is appropriate, but no authoritative source with a precise locator is supplied.

knowledge_statements.title: Last-Iterate Residual Rates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonergodic residual bound for an averaged fixed-point iteration with a nonempty fixed-point set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H\) be a Hilbert space, let \(T:H\to H\) be \(\alpha\)-averaged with \(0<\alpha<1\), and generate \(z^{k+1}=Tz^k\). If \(F=\operatorname{Fix}T\neq\varnothing\), then the last-iterate residual \(r_k=\|z^{k+1}-z^k\|\) is nonincreasing and satisfies
\[
r_k\leq \sqrt{\frac{\alpha}{(1-\alpha)(k+1)}}\,\operatorname{dist}(z^0,F).
\]
Moreover, \(r_k=o(k^{-1/2})\). Thus obtaining \(r_k\leq\varepsilon\) requires at most \(O(\varepsilon^{-2})\) iterations under this fixed-point oracle model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an averaged fixed-point iteration, the current—not merely best—residual is at most a constant times the initial solution distance divided by the square root of the iteration count.
assumptions_latex: \(T\) is \(\alpha\)-averaged for some \(0<\alpha<1\).
\(\operatorname{Fix}T\neq\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\|z^{k+1}-z^k\|=o(k^{-1/2})\), with the displayed explicit \(O(k^{-1/2})\) bound.

notation.meaning: fixed-point set of the iteration map

knowledge_statements.title: Embedding Fixed-Point Residual Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: ADMM or Douglas–Rachford residual bound measured directly in homogeneous self-dual embedding coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let the homogeneous self-dual embedding iteration be represented as \(w^{k+1}=Tw^k\) on a finite-dimensional Hilbert space with norm \(\|\cdot\|_M\), where \(M\succ0\), \(T\) is firmly nonexpansive in that norm, and \(F=\operatorname{Fix}T\neq\varnothing\). For the embedding residual \(r_k^{\mathrm{emb}}=\|w^{k+1}-w^k\|_M\),
\[
r_k^{\mathrm{emb}}\leq\frac{\operatorname{dist}_M(w^0,F)}{\sqrt{k+1}},
\qquad r_k^{\mathrm{emb}}=o(k^{-1/2}).
\]
Consequently an embedding fixed-point residual at most \(\varepsilon\) is reached within \(O(\varepsilon^{-2})\) iterations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A firmly nonexpansive embedding iteration has a last-iterate fixed-point residual decaying at least as the inverse square root of the iteration count.
assumptions_latex: \(M\succ0\) and \(T\) is firmly nonexpansive in \(\|\cdot\|_M\).
\(\operatorname{Fix}T\neq\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(r_k^{\mathrm{emb}}\leq\operatorname{dist}_M(w^0,F)/\sqrt{k+1}\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The cited self-dual-embedding section does not by itself establish that the particular embedding iteration is firmly nonexpansive in the stated metric or support the displayed last-iterate rate. An exact ADMM or Douglas–Rachford theorem with an inspectable locator is required.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditional transfer of an embedding fixed-point residual bound to normalized primal and dual conic diagnostics.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose an embedding point \(w\) yields a scalar \(\tau(w)>0\) and recovered variables \(x(w),y(w),s(w)\). Let \(R_{\rm con}(w)\) collect primal feasibility, dual feasibility, cone-membership, and duality-gap residuals after normalization by \(\tau(w)\). Assume that, on the iterates under consideration, \(\tau(w^k)\geq\tau_{\min}>0\) and
\[
\|R_{\rm con}(w^k)\|\leq \frac{L}{\tau(w^k)}\|w^{k+1}-w^k\|_M.
\]
Then
\[
\|R_{\rm con}(w^k)\|\leq \frac{L}{\tau_{\min}}\|w^{k+1}-w^k\|_M.
\]
Consequently, under this transfer inequality, any \(O(k^{-1/2})\) embedding residual bound yields an \(O(k^{-1/2})\) recovered conic residual bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the homogeneous recovery scale is uniformly positive and the recovered diagnostics satisfy the stated transfer inequality, they inherit the embedding residual rate with a constant amplified by the inverse lower bound on that scale.
knowledge_statements.title: Recovered Conic Residual Bounds

knowledge_statements.title: Difference-Sequence Rates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Asymptotic infeasibility direction from successive differences of a fixed-point iteration without attainable fixed points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(T:H\to H\) be averaged on a finite-dimensional Hilbert space, generate \(z^{k+1}=Tz^k\), and define the minimal displacement vector \(v=P_{\overline{\operatorname{ran}(I-T)}}(0)\). Then
\[
z^{k+1}-z^k\longrightarrow -v.
\]
When \(v\neq0\), the limiting difference supplies a separating or infeasibility direction after problem-specific decoding. Averagedness alone gives no uniform numerical convergence rate for \(\|(z^{k+1}-z^k)+v\|\); a rate requires additional regularity such as metric subregularity, polyhedrality, or an error bound for the displacement mapping.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Successive iterate differences converge to the negative minimal displacement vector, but averagedness alone supplies no uniform rate for this infeasibility-direction convergence.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is finite-dimensional and \(T\) is averaged.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(z^{k+1}-z^k\to-v\), with no uniform rate under averagedness alone.

notation.meaning: minimal displacement vector of the fixed-point map
Euclidean projection onto a closed convex set

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The statement fits a failure-boundary treatment of difference-sequence rates, but neither convergence to the minimal displacement vector nor the stronger absence of a uniform numerical rate is supported by a cited source. The problem-specific infeasibility decoding also requires a qualified source.

assumptions_latex: \(\|d_i+v\|\leq\epsilon_i\) for a nonnegative sequence \((\epsilon_i)_{i\geq0}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantitative rate transfer from successive-difference errors to the normalized iterate displacement.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose \(d_i=z^{i+1}-z^i\to-v\). Then, for every integer \(k\geq1\),
\[
\frac{z^k-z^0}{k}+v=\frac1k\sum_{i=0}^{k-1}(d_i+v),
\qquad \frac{z^k-z^0}{k}\longrightarrow-v.
\]
If \(\|d_i+v\|\leq\epsilon_i\) for all \(i\geq0\), then
\[
\left\|\frac{z^k-z^0}{k}+v\right\|\leq\frac1k\sum_{i=0}^{k-1}\epsilon_i.
\]
Thus, if \(\epsilon_i=O((i+1)^{-p})\), the normalized error is \(O(k^{-p})\) for \(0<p<1\), \(O((\log k)/k)\) for \(p=1\), and \(O(k^{-1})\) for \(p>1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The normalized iterate displacement is the average of the successive differences. Therefore its directional error is bounded by the average difference-sequence error, with the stated polynomial and logarithmic rate transfers.
knowledge_statements.title: Normalized-Sequence Rates

knowledge_statements.title: Primal–Dual Gap Rates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ergodic restricted-gap rate for primal–dual splitting of a finite-dimensional conic saddle problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider the saddle function \(L(x,y)=f(x)+\langle Ax,y\rangle-g^*(y)\), where \(f\) and \(g^*\) are proper closed convex functions. Let primal–dual hybrid gradient use constant steps \(\tau,\sigma>0\) satisfying \(\tau\sigma\|A\|^2<1\), and let \((\bar x^k,\bar y^k)\) be the arithmetic averages of its first \(k\) iterates. For bounded test sets \(B_x,B_y\), define
\[
\mathcal G_B(x,y)=\sup_{y'\in B_y}L(x,y')-\inf_{x'\in B_x}L(x',y).
\]
Then \(\mathcal G_B(\bar x^k,\bar y^k)\leq C_B/k\), where \(C_B<\infty\) depends on the initialization, steps, and test sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For stable primal–dual splitting, the restricted primal–dual gap of arithmetic-average iterates decreases as one over the iteration count.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) and \(g^*\) are proper, closed, and convex.
\(B_x\) and \(B_y\) are bounded.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal G_B(\bar x^k,\bar y^k)\leq C_B/k\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: An ergodic restricted-gap complexity bound is appropriate for this terminal, but the exact PDHG update and averaging convention are not specified, and no source supports the displayed theorem under precisely the listed hypotheses. The mathematical version cannot be fixed reliably without the intended theorem.

knowledge_statements.title: Iterate Convergence Rates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Residual convergence does not by itself control distance of current iterates from the solution set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(0<\varepsilon<1\), let \(T_\varepsilon:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) be \(T_\varepsilon x=(1-\varepsilon)x\). Its fixed-point set is \(F=\{0\}\), and the iteration satisfies
\[
\operatorname{dist}(x^k,F)=(1-\varepsilon)^k|x^0|,
\qquad \|x^k-T_\varepsilon x^k\|=\varepsilon\operatorname{dist}(x^k,F).
\]
Although every \(T_\varepsilon\) is averaged and the residual can be arbitrarily small relative to iterate error, the contraction factor approaches one as \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\). Hence no uniform iterate-distance rate follows from averagedness and residual decay alone; an error-bound modulus is necessary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A small fixed-point residual need not mean a nearby solution: simple averaged contractions can converge arbitrarily slowly as their error-bound constant deteriorates.
assumptions_latex: \(0<\varepsilon<1\).
\(x^{k+1}=T_\varepsilon x^k\) with \(T_\varepsilon x=(1-\varepsilon)x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: No uniform iterate-distance rate follows from averagedness and residual decay alone.

knowledge_statements.title: Strong-Monotonicity Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global linear convergence of the proximal-point fixed-point map under strong monotonicity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\) be maximally \(\mu\)-strongly monotone on a Hilbert space, with \(\mu>0\), and let \(z^\star\) be its unique zero. For \(\gamma>0\), the resolvent \(J_{\gamma A}=(I+\gamma A)^{-1}\) is Lipschitz with constant \(q=(1+\gamma\mu)^{-1}<1\). Therefore the proximal-point iteration \(z^{k+1}=J_{\gamma A}z^k\) obeys
\[
\|z^k-z^\star\|\leq q^k\|z^0-z^\star\|.
\]
It reaches iterate error at most \(\varepsilon\) after \(O((\gamma\mu)^{-1}\log(1/\varepsilon))\) iterations when \(\gamma\mu\) is bounded above.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong monotonicity makes the proximal fixed-point map contractive, yielding global geometric convergence to the unique solution.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) is maximally \(\mu\)-strongly monotone with \(\mu>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\|z^k-z^\star\|\leq(1+\gamma\mu)^{-k}\|z^0-z^\star\|\).
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The resolvent contraction and geometric iterate bound are standard and the complexity-bound kind fits the enhanced-rate regime, but no inspectable authoritative source is supplied for the exact hypotheses and rate statement.

knowledge_statements.title: Metric-Subregularity Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local linear convergence of an averaged fixed-point iteration under a residual error bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(T:H\to H\) be \(\alpha\)-averaged, let \(F=\operatorname{Fix}T\neq\varnothing\), and suppose a neighborhood \(U\) of \(F\) is invariant under \(T\). If the residual mapping \(R=I-T\) is metrically subregular on \(U\) with
\[
\operatorname{dist}(z,F)\leq\kappa\|Rz\|,
\]
then every iterate in \(U\) satisfies
\[
\operatorname{dist}(Tz,F)^2\leq\left(1-\frac{1-\alpha}{\alpha\kappa^2}\right)\operatorname{dist}(z,F)^2.
\]
Whenever the displayed factor lies in \([0,1)\), the fixed-point iterates converge locally Q-linearly in distance to \(F\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An error bound converting residual size into solution distance upgrades averaged fixed-point descent to local linear convergence.
assumptions_latex: \(T\) is \(\alpha\)-averaged and \(F=\operatorname{Fix}T\neq\varnothing\).
\(U\) is invariant and \(\operatorname{dist}(z,F)\leq\kappa\|(I-T)z\|\) on \(U\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{dist}(z^{k+1},F)\leq q\operatorname{dist}(z^k,F)\), where \(q=\sqrt{1-(1-\alpha)/(\alpha\kappa^2)}<1\).
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The residual error bound combined with averaged-map descent gives the displayed local distance contraction, and property is a reasonable role for this regime. An authoritative source is nevertheless required for the precise metric-subregularity formulation, locality assumptions, and contraction factor.

knowledge_statements.title: Polyhedral Error-Bound Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local linear convergence induced by a Hoffman-type bound for a polyhedral fixed-point residual map.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(T:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n\) be \(\alpha\)-averaged and piecewise affine, and assume \(F=\operatorname{Fix}T\neq\varnothing\). The residual mapping \(R=I-T\) is piecewise polyhedral; hence, on every bounded neighborhood \(U\) of a reference fixed point, there exists \(\kappa_U<\infty\) such that
\[
\operatorname{dist}(z,F)\leq\kappa_U\|Rz\|\quad(z\in U).
\]
If the iterates remain in \(U\), averaged-map descent gives local Q-linear convergence of their distances to \(F\), with admissible factor
\[
q_U=\sqrt{1-\frac{1-\alpha}{\alpha\kappa_U^2}}<1
\]
whenever the expression is real.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A piecewise-affine averaged map has a local polyhedral error bound, which converts fixed-point descent into local geometric convergence.
assumptions_latex: \(T\) is piecewise affine and \(\alpha\)-averaged.
\(F=\operatorname{Fix}T\neq\varnothing\).
The iterates remain in a bounded error-bound neighborhood \(U\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{dist}(z^{k+1},F)\leq q_U\operatorname{dist}(z^k,F)\) locally for some \(q_U<1\).
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The claimed route from a piecewise-affine averaged map through a polyhedral error bound to local linear convergence is plausible and locally appropriate, but no source supports the asserted bounded-neighborhood error bound or its use with the exact contraction factor.

knowledge_statements.title: Strict-Complementarity Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Face-based strict complementarity for a primal–dual solution of a finite-dimensional conic program.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider a primal–dual feasible pair with \(x^\star\in K\), dual slack \(s^\star\in K^*\), and \(\langle x^\star,s^\star\rangle=0\), where \(K\) is a closed convex cone. Let \(F\) be the minimal face of \(K\) containing \(x^\star\), and define its complementary face by \(F^\triangle=K^*\cap F^\perp\). The pair is strictly complementary precisely when
\[
x^\star\in\operatorname{ri}F
\quad\text{and}\quad
s^\star\in\operatorname{ri}F^\triangle.
\]
For the semidefinite cone this is equivalent to \(\operatorname{rank}(X^\star)+\operatorname{rank}(S^\star)=n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strict complementarity places the primal point and dual slack in the relative interiors of complementary faces; for semidefinite programs, their ranks sum to the matrix dimension.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a finite-dimensional closed convex cone.
\(x^\star\in K\), \(s^\star\in K^*\), and \(\langle x^\star,s^\star\rangle=0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^\star\in\operatorname{ri}F\) and \(s^\star\in\operatorname{ri}(K^*\cap F^\perp)\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primal conic nondegeneracy expressed as surjectivity along the tangent-cone lineality space.

source_refs.locator: 3.3.1 Facial structure, nondegeneracy and strict complementarity p. 37

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the conic system \(\mathcal A x=b\), \(x\in K\), let \(x^\star\) be feasible and let \(T_K(x^\star)\) denote the tangent cone. The primal solution is nondegenerate when the constraint map is surjective on the lineality space of the tangent cone:
\[
\mathcal A\bigl(\operatorname{lin}T_K(x^\star)\bigr)=\mathbb R^m.
\]
Equivalently, if \(y\in\mathbb R^m\) and
\[
\mathcal A^*y\in\bigl(\operatorname{lin}T_K(x^\star)\bigr)^\perp,
\]
then \(y=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Primal nondegeneracy requires equality-constraint perturbations to be generated by two-sided tangent directions at the conic solution. Equivalently, no nonzero equality multiplier has an adjoint image orthogonal to all such directions.

knowledge_statements.title: Level-Set Geometry Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Error-bound formulation of favorable geometry on a bounded objective level set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, closed, and convex on a finite-dimensional Hilbert space, with nonempty solution set \(X^*=\operatorname*{argmin}f\). A level set \(L_\alpha=\{x:f(x)\leq\alpha\}\), where \(\alpha>f^*\), has favorable level-set geometry of order \(p\geq1\) if there exists \(\kappa>0\) such that \[\operatorname{dist}(x,X^*)^p\leq\kappa\bigl(f(x)-f^*\bigr)\qquad\text{for every }x\in L_\alpha.\] This condition converts objective residual control into distance-to-solution control throughout the specified level set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A level set is geometrically regular when objective error uniformly bounds a positive power of the distance to the solution set.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is finite-dimensional.
\(f\) is proper, closed, and convex with \(X^*\neq\varnothing\).
\(\alpha>f^*=\min f\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{dist}(x,X^*)\leq\bigl(\kappa(f(x)-f^*)\bigr)^{1/p}\) for every \(x\in L_\alpha\).

knowledge_statements.title: Inexact Affine-Solve Convergence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Perturbed averaged-splitting convergence under summable affine-solve errors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T:H\to H\) be an averaged operator with \(\operatorname{Fix}T\neq\varnothing\), representing one exact conic-splitting step. Suppose the affine-system subproblem at iteration \(k\) is solved inexactly, producing \[z^{k+1}=Tz^k+e_A^k,\qquad \sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\lVert e_A^k\rVert<\infty.\] Then \((z^k)\) converges in finite dimensions to some \(z^*\in\operatorname{Fix}T\), and \(\lVert z^k-Tz^k\rVert\to0\). Thus summably inaccurate affine solves preserve the fixed-point convergence conclusion of the exact splitting method.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An averaged conic splitting iteration still converges when the additive errors caused by its affine solves are absolutely summable.

\(T\) is averaged and \(\operatorname{Fix}T\neq\varnothing\).

knowledge_statements.title: Inexact Cone-Projection Convergence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional perturbed averaged-splitting convergence under summable cone-projection errors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H\) be a finite-dimensional Hilbert space, let \(K\subseteq H\) be a nonempty closed convex cone, and let \(T:H\to H\) be the averaged fixed-point operator of an exact conic splitting scheme, with \(\operatorname{Fix}T\neq\varnothing\). At iteration \(k\), suppose \(p^k\) approximates the exact projection of \(v^k\) and the resulting splitting step satisfies \[\lVert p^k-\Pi_K(v^k)\rVert\leq\eta_k,\qquad z^{k+1}=Tz^k+e_K^k,\qquad \lVert e_K^k\rVert\leq C\eta_k,\] for a constant \(C\geq0\). If \(\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\eta_k<\infty\), then \(z^k\to z^*\) for some \(z^*\in\operatorname{Fix}T\), and \(\lVert z^k-Tz^k\rVert\to0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In finite dimensions, approximate cone projections preserve convergence of an averaged splitting iteration when the induced additive step errors are bounded by a summable tolerance sequence.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a finite-dimensional Hilbert space.
\(K\subseteq H\) is a nonempty closed convex cone.
\(T:H\to H\) is averaged and \(\operatorname{Fix}T\neq\varnothing\).
\(\lVert e_K^k\rVert\leq C\eta_k\) for some \(C\geq0\), and \(\sum_k\eta_k<\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(z^k\to z^*\in\operatorname{Fix}T\) and \(\lVert z^k-Tz^k\rVert\to0\).

notation.meaning: Projection input and its approximate projected value at iteration k.
Additive perturbation induced in the splitting step.
Uniform constant relating projection error to step error.
