knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates absence of a reliable conclusion from assertions of infeasibility, unboundedness, or nonexistence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P_{\mathrm{accept}}\) be the disjunction of every documented accurate or inaccurate solution, infeasibility-certificate, and unboundedness-certificate predicate. If the solver stops with \(P_{\mathrm{accept}}=\mathrm{false}\), it may report an indeterminate status. Typical triggers include nonfinite arithmetic, numerical breakdown, stagnation, or residuals outside all acceptance thresholds, but none is itself a proof about the conic program. The solver must retain the stopping reason and available residuals; indeterminate must not be translated into infeasible, unbounded, or no-solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Indeterminate means the solver stopped without validating any documented solution or certificate predicate; it is not evidence for infeasibility, unboundedness, or nonexistence.
knowledge_statements.title: Indeterminate Statuses

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role is appropriate and the noncommittal interpretation is sensible, but the exhaustive acceptance disjunction, included triggers, and reporting requirements are solver-interface policies without cited support.

children.title: Ambiguous Status Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Diagnostic regimes where nearby status classifications cannot be cleanly distinguished.

assumptions_latex: The original conic problem is \(\inf\{c^\top x:Ax=b,\ x\in K\}\), where \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is a closed convex cone.
Nonnegative tolerances \(\varepsilon_{\rm sol},\varepsilon_{\rm inf},\varepsilon_{\rm unb}\) and corresponding validation predicates are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex:
A termination report lies on an ambiguous status boundary when its returned data satisfy none of the validated predicates for an approximate primal-dual solution, a primal-infeasibility certificate, or an unboundedness direction, or when finite-precision evaluations make two logically incompatible predicates pass. Concretely, the diagnostic status is indeterminate whenever \(
eg V_{m sol}\land
eg V_{m inf}\land
eg V_{m unb}\), and it is contradictory whenever at least two of \(V_{m sol},V_{m inf},V_{m unb}\) hold although their exact counterparts are mutually exclusive. Such a report must not be interpreted as a mathematical solution or certificate without revalidation.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: numerical solver statuses require explicit, mutually consistent validation predicates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-precision boundary between inaccurate, contradictory, and indeterminate conic-solver reports.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(P=\inf\{c^\top x:Ax=b,\ x\in K\}\), fix Boolean validation predicates \(V_{\rm sol}\), \(V_{\rm inf}\), and \(V_{\rm unb}\) for an approximate solution, an infeasibility certificate, and an improving recession direction. The report is diagnostically ambiguous if
\[
\neg V_{\rm sol}\land\neg V_{\rm inf}\land\neg V_{\rm unb},
\]
or if finite-precision tests accept two predicates whose exact versions are logically incompatible. In either case, no definite mathematical status follows from the solver label alone; the output remains indeterminate until original-scale or higher-precision validation selects one consistent predicate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A solver report is ambiguous when no solution or certificate test passes, or numerical error makes incompatible tests pass. The reported label then has no mathematical force without revalidation.
knowledge_statements.title: Ambiguous Status Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role and predicate-based formulation fit the terminal container, and the notation is internally consistent. However, no inspectable citation supports the proposed taxonomy of indeterminate and contradictory finite-precision statuses, so the status semantics remain source-dependent.

assumptions_latex: The solver used known invertible primal and dual changes of variables and known nonzero row, column, and objective scalings.
The unscaled problem is \(\inf\{c^\top x:Ax=b,\ x\in K\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The candidate is accepted only according to residuals, cone distances, objective gap, and certificate inequalities recomputed from \((A,b,c,K)\) after undoing every solver scaling.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: residual validation must be performed in the coordinates of the stated problem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Validation after exactly reversing presolve and numerical equilibration transformations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Input the original data \((A,b,c,K)\), the solver output \((\widehat x,\widehat y,\widehat s)\), and every recorded scaling or affine transformation. First invert those transformations to obtain \((x,y,s)\) in the original coordinates. Recompute, without reusing scaled residuals,
\[
r_p=Ax-b,\qquad s=c-A^\top y,\qquad g=c^\top x-b^\top y,
\]
together with \(\operatorname{dist}(x,K)\) and \(\operatorname{dist}(s,K^*)\). Reconstruct and test any infeasibility or unboundedness certificate against the original data. Output valid only when the designated original-scale absolute or relative tolerances all hold; otherwise output validation failed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Undo all solver transformations, then recompute feasibility, cone membership, gap, and certificate tests using the original problem data and tolerances.
knowledge_statements.title: Original-Scale Rechecking

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithmic role fits original-scale rechecking, and the stated residuals are consistent with the declared primal-dual convention. An authoritative source is still required for the transformation-reversal and validation procedure, including treatment of presolve transformations and relative tolerances.

assumptions_latex: The cone \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty and closed.
A norm \(\|\cdot\|\) and membership tolerance \(\varepsilon_K\ge 0\) are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exact membership is equivalent to \(d_K(z)=0\); numerical membership at tolerance \(\varepsilon_K\) is the checkable condition \(d_K(z)\le\varepsilon_K\).

notation.meaning: distance from a candidate to the cone

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: distance to a closed set gives an exact and tolerance-based membership test
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Norm-based validation applicable to primal cones and dual cones.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a candidate \(z\in\mathbb R^n\), define
\[
d_K(z):=\inf_{u\in K}\|z-u\|.
\]
Because \(K\) is closed, \(z\in K\) if and only if \(d_K(z)=0\). A numerical cone-membership test at tolerance \(\varepsilon_K\) accepts precisely when \(d_K(z)\le\varepsilon_K\). For a product cone \(K=K_1\times\cdots\times K_q\), every block must be checked in its declared cone, using compatible block norms or a stated aggregate norm. The same rule validates a dual slack by replacing \(K\) with \(K^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Validate cone membership by computing distance to the declared cone. Exact membership means zero distance; numerical acceptance requires distance no larger than the stated tolerance.
knowledge_statements.title: Cone-Membership Validation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The distance condition is mathematically correct for a nonempty closed cone and fits cone-membership validation. No inspectable source is supplied for the numerical validation prescription, especially its product-cone and norm-aggregation conventions.

assumptions_latex: The original conic data and candidate can be represented in arithmetic of precision higher than that used by the solver.
A validation tolerance and a precision-escalation limit are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The candidate is validated only if independently recomputed higher-precision quantities satisfy the prescribed tests stably under at least one further precision increase.

notation.meaning: working arithmetic precision at validation stage \(j\)
vector of recomputed diagnostic quantities at precision \(p_j\)

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: precision escalation distinguishes arithmetic artifacts from stable residual violations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Precision-escalating residual and certificate validation, not a new optimization solve.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input original-scale data, a candidate solution or certificate, initial precision \(p_0\), tolerance \(\varepsilon\), and maximum precision \(p_{\max}\). At precision \(p_j\), independently recompute all affine residuals, objective gaps, cone distances, and certificate signs from the original data, obtaining \(R_{p_j}\). Increase precision, for example by \(p_{j+1}=2p_j\), until either the required inequalities hold and their truth values remain unchanged at \(p_{j+1}\), or \(p_{\max}\) is reached. Output validated in the first case and unresolved in the second; output invalid if a tolerance is stably violated.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Recompute every diagnostic in higher precision and increase precision again. Accept only when all tests pass and their truth values remain stable.
knowledge_statements.title: Higher-Precision Validation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits the terminal container, but the proposed requirement that truth values remain unchanged after one further precision increase is a particular validation policy rather than a source-independent mathematical standard. A source is needed to establish the escalation and termination rules.

assumptions_latex: Two implementations solve the same original-scale conic problem and expose candidates that can be checked independently.
Common validation tolerances and status predicates are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Agreement is corroborating evidence only when both independently returned objects pass common original-data tests; disagreement or unvalidated agreement triggers an unresolved assessment.

notation.meaning: common original-scale validation predicate for status \(\sigma\)

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: implementation diversity can reveal solver-specific numerical failures but does not replace certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cross-checking solver outputs under common predicates; agreement alone is not certification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let independent solvers return \((\sigma_1,z^{(1)})\) and \((\sigma_2,z^{(2)})\) for the same unscaled data. Cross-validation succeeds only if \(\sigma_1=\sigma_2=\sigma\) and both \(V_\sigma(z^{(1)})\) and \(V_\sigma(z^{(2)})\) hold when recomputed from the original problem. For solution statuses, additionally compare objective values and, when uniqueness is expected, candidate variables under stated tolerances. If the statuses disagree, either object fails validation, or agreement occurs without a passing predicate, the result is unresolved. Independent agreement increases diagnostic confidence but is not by itself a proof of the reported status.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two solvers corroborate a status only when both outputs independently pass the same original-data tests. Mere agreement is not a certificate; disagreement remains unresolved.
knowledge_statements.title: Independent-Solver Cross-Validation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The principle correctly distinguishes corroboration from certification and fits independent-solver cross-validation. The record has no inspectable citation supporting its success and unresolved-status criteria.

children.title: Certificate Validity Assessment
children.top_down_role: Validation concerns specific to reported infeasibility or unboundedness certificates.

assumptions_latex: The primal conic problem is \(\inf\{c^\top x:Ax=b,\ x\in K\}\), with closed convex cone \(K\).
The proposed certificate is evaluated in original coordinates with fixed tolerances.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An exact vector satisfying the applicable displayed predicate certifies primal infeasibility or primal unboundedness; an approximate vector is valid only under a separately specified robust tolerance rule that preserves the strict conclusion.

notation.meaning: feasible base point and improving recession direction

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: conic alternatives and recession directions provide directly checkable exact certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact infeasibility and unboundedness certificates for standard equality-form conic programs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(K^*:=\{z\in\mathbb R^n:z^\top x\ge0\text{ for every }x\in K\}\), a proposed primal-infeasibility certificate \(y\in\mathbb R^m\) is valid when
\[
A^\top y\in K^*,\qquad b^\top y<0.
\]
A proposed primal-unboundedness certificate is a pair \((x_0,d)\in\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^n\) satisfying
\[
Ax_0=b,\quad x_0\in K,\quad Ad=0,\quad d\in K,\quad c^\top d<0.
\]
Certificate validity assessment recomputes every equality, cone-membership condition, and strict sign from the original-scale data. Approximate satisfaction is accepted only under a stated error rule that guarantees preservation of the required strict inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A primal-infeasibility certificate must satisfy the dual-cone and negative-pairing conditions. A primal-unboundedness certificate must provide a feasible base point and a cone-feasible improving recession direction. All conditions must be re-evaluated in original coordinates.
knowledge_statements.title: Certificate Validity Assessment

children.title: Candidate Solution Validity Assessment
children.top_down_role: Validation concerns specific to reported primal–dual solution candidates.

assumptions_latex: The primal-dual pair is \(\inf\{c^\top x:Ax=b,\ x\in K\}\) and \(\sup\{b^\top y:c-A^\top y\in K^*\}\).
Absolute or relative tolerances for feasibility, cone distance, and duality gap are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The candidate is valid at the declared tolerances exactly when all primal feasibility, dual feasibility, cone-membership, and gap tests pass in original coordinates.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: KKT residuals and cone distances are standard a posteriori checks for primal-dual candidates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tolerance-based a posteriori validity for a primal-dual candidate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given \((x,y)\), form \(s=c-A^\top y\) and \(g=c^\top x-b^\top y\). Under absolute tolerances \(\varepsilon_p,\varepsilon_K,\varepsilon_g\ge0\), the candidate is valid when
\[
\|Ax-b\|\le\varepsilon_p,\quad \operatorname{dist}(x,K)\le\varepsilon_K,\quad \operatorname{dist}(s,K^*)\le\varepsilon_K,\quad |g|\le\varepsilon_g.
\]
For relative tests, each left-hand side is divided by a declared scale bounded away from zero. All quantities must be recomputed from original-scale data. Passing these tests establishes only validity at the stated tolerances, not exact feasibility or exact optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A primal-dual candidate is valid at stated tolerances when original-scale affine residuals, cone distances, and objective gap all satisfy their declared bounds.
knowledge_statements.title: Candidate Solution Validity Assessment

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition role fits candidate-solution assessment, and the residual, cone-distance, and gap tests are consistent with the stated primal-dual pair. The exact normalization and acceptance policy are implementation-sensitive and have no inspectable supporting citation.

assumptions_latex: Problem data \(d=(A,b,c)\) lie in a normed data space \(\mathcal D\).
The ill-posed set \(\Sigma\) is the boundary across which the relevant feasibility or boundedness status changes.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A feasible datum is well-conditioned when \(\delta(d):=\operatorname{dist}(d,\Sigma)>0\); perturbations smaller than \(\delta(d)\) cannot cross the status boundary.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Normwise distance-to-ill-posedness classification for feasible conic data.

source_refs.locator: 3.3 The geometry of cone-lp's: main results p. 37

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(d=(A,b,c)\in\mathcal D\) describe a conic program and let \(\Sigma\subseteq\mathcal D\) be the boundary separating data with distinct feasibility or boundedness statuses. Define
\[
\delta(d):=\operatorname{dist}(d,\Sigma)=\inf_{\bar d\in\Sigma}\|d-\bar d\|.
\]
A feasible datum \(d\) is in the well-conditioned feasible regime when \(\delta(d)>0\). Consequently, every perturbation \(\Delta d\) satisfying \(\|\Delta d\|<\delta(d)\) remains on the same side of the relevant status boundary. When \(\|d\|>0\), the associated normwise condition ratio is \(\|d\|/\delta(d)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible conic problem is well-conditioned when it has positive distance from the boundary where feasibility or boundedness status can change.
knowledge_statements.title: Well-Conditioned Feasible Regime

source_witnesses.locator: 3.3 The geometry of cone-lp's: main results p. 37

assumptions_latex: Problem data \(d\) belong to a normed data space \(\mathcal D\), and \(F\) and \(I\) denote its feasible and infeasible data sets.
A dimensionless threshold \(\eta>0\) is fixed and \(\|d\|>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A feasible datum is nearly infeasible at threshold \(\eta\) when \(0<\operatorname{dist}(d,I)\le\eta\|d\|\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantitative feasible-side neighborhood of the infeasibility boundary.

source_refs.locator: 3.3 The geometry of cone-lp's: main results p. 37

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F,I\subseteq\mathcal D\) be the feasible and infeasible subsets of a normed conic-data space \(\mathcal D\). For a chosen dimensionless threshold \(\eta>0\), a datum \(d\in F\) with \(\|d\|>0\) is nearly infeasible when
\[
0<\operatorname{dist}(d,I)\le\eta\|d\|.
\]
Equivalently, for every \(\epsilon>0\), there exists \(d'\in I\) such that \(\|d'-d\|\le\eta\|d\|+\epsilon\), while the unperturbed datum remains feasible. The strict lower bound excludes feasible data having zero distance from \(I\). The classification depends on the declared data norm, perturbation model, and threshold \(\eta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible problem is nearly infeasible when its positive distance to the infeasible data set is no greater than a declared fraction of the data norm. Infeasible data can then be approached within that relative distance, up to an arbitrarily small excess.
knowledge_statements.title: Nearly Infeasible Regime

source_witnesses.locator: 3.3 The geometry of cone-lp's: main results p. 37

assumptions_latex: Problem data \(d\) belong to a normed data space \(\mathcal D\), and \(B\) and \(U\) denote its finite-valued and primal-unbounded data sets.
A dimensionless threshold \(\eta>0\) is fixed and \(\|d\|>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A finite-valued datum is nearly unbounded at threshold \(\eta\) when \(0<\operatorname{dist}(d,U)\le\eta\|d\|\).

notation.meaning: data with finite primal optimal value
data for which the primal objective is unbounded below

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-valued-side neighborhood of the primal-unboundedness boundary.

source_refs.locator: 3.3 The geometry of cone-lp's: main results p. 37

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(B,U\subseteq\mathcal D\) be the subsets of a normed conic-data space \(\mathcal D\) having, respectively, a finite primal optimal value and a primal objective unbounded below. For a chosen dimensionless threshold \(\eta>0\), a datum \(d\in B\) with \(\|d\|>0\) is nearly unbounded when
\[
0<\operatorname{dist}(d,U)\le\eta\|d\|.
\]
Equivalently, for every \(\epsilon>0\), there exists \(d'\in U\) such that \(\|d'-d\|\le\eta\|d\|+\epsilon\), while the unperturbed datum has finite primal value. The strict lower bound excludes finite-valued data having zero distance from \(U\). This regime depends on the declared data norm, perturbation model, and threshold \(\eta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite-valued problem is nearly unbounded when its positive distance to the primal-unbounded data set is no greater than a declared fraction of the data norm. Unbounded data can then be approached within that relative distance, up to an arbitrarily small excess.
knowledge_statements.title: Nearly Unbounded Regime

source_witnesses.locator: 3.3 The geometry of cone-lp's: main results p. 37

assumptions_latex: Problem data lie in a normed space \(\mathcal D\).
The set \(\Sigma\) is the boundary between data having different relevant conic statuses.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The ill-posed boundary regime is exactly \(d\in\Sigma\), equivalently \(\operatorname{dist}(d,\Sigma)=0\) when \(\Sigma\) is closed.

notation.meaning: closed status boundary in data space

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Zero-distance boundary where arbitrarily small perturbations may change conic status.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\Sigma\subseteq\mathcal D\) be the closed boundary separating data with different feasibility or boundedness statuses. A datum \(d\) is in the ill-posed boundary regime precisely when
\[
d\in\Sigma,
\]
equivalently when \(\delta(d):=\operatorname{dist}(d,\Sigma)=0\). Hence, for every \(\varepsilon>0\), there are data \(d'\) with \(\|d'-d\|<\varepsilon\) lying arbitrarily near, and under a genuine status-separating boundary on opposite sides, of distinct status regions. No positive perturbation radius can guarantee preservation of status at such a datum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Ill-posed data lie exactly on a status boundary, so no positive perturbation radius guarantees that feasibility or boundedness status will remain unchanged.
knowledge_statements.title: Ill-Posed Boundary Regime

assumptions_latex: The feasibility system is \(Ax=b\), \(x\in K\), where \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is a closed convex cone with nonempty interior.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The system is strongly feasible exactly when the affine set \(\{x:Ax=b\}\) intersects \(\operatorname{int}K\).

notation.meaning: interior of the cone in its ambient space

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ambient-interior version of strong feasibility for equality-form conic systems.

source_refs.locator: 3.3 The geometry of cone-lp's: main results p. 37

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a closed convex cone \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) with \(\operatorname{int}K\ne\varnothing\), the conic system
\[
Ax=b,\qquad x\in K
\]
is strongly feasible if there exists \(\bar x\in\operatorname{int}K\) such that \(A\bar x=b\). Equivalently, with \(L:=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax=b\}\), strong feasibility is the condition \(L\cap\operatorname{int}K\ne\varnothing\). This is strict primal feasibility. It is distinct from mere feasibility, which permits every feasible point to lie on \(\partial K\), and from simultaneous primal-dual strict feasibility, which additionally imposes the analogous condition on the dual system.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cone program is strongly feasible when its affine constraints admit a point in the interior of the cone, rather than only on its boundary.
knowledge_statements.title: Strongly Feasible Cone Programs

source_witnesses.locator: 3.3 The geometry of cone-lp's: main results p. 37

knowledge_statements.title: Weakly Feasible Cone Programs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasibility classification relative to the cone’s relative interior.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(E,F\) be finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces, let \(K\subseteq E\) be a nonempty closed convex cone, let \(A:E\to F\) be linear, and let \(b\in F\). The conic system \(Ax=b\), \(x\in K\), is weakly feasible when
\[
\{x\in K:Ax=b\}\neq\varnothing
\quad\text{and}\quad
\{x\in\operatorname{ri}K:Ax=b\}=\varnothing.
\]
Thus feasibility holds, but the affine constraint set does not meet the relative interior of the original cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cone program is weakly feasible when it has a feasible point but no feasible point in the cone’s relative interior.
assumptions_latex: \(E,F\) are finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces.
\(K\subseteq E\) is a nonempty closed convex cone.
\(A:E\to F\) is linear and \(b\in F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K\cap\{x:Ax=b\}\neq\varnothing\) and \(\operatorname{ri}K\cap\{x:Ax=b\}=\varnothing\).

notation.meaning: relative interior of the cone K

knowledge_statements.title: Strongly Infeasible Cone Programs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Image-space definition with a strict conic separation certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(K\subseteq E\) be a nonempty closed convex cone, let \(A:E\to F\) be linear, and let \(b\in F\). The system \(Ax=b\), \(x\in K\), is strongly infeasible when
\[
\operatorname{dist}\bigl(b,A(K)\bigr)>0,
\]
equivalently, when \(b\notin\operatorname{cl}A(K)\). In finite dimensions this is equivalent to the existence of \(y\in F\) satisfying
\[
A^*y\in K^*,\qquad \langle b,y\rangle<0,
\]
which strictly separates \(b\) from the conic image.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong infeasibility means the right-hand side has positive distance from the conic image, equivalently admitting a strict separating dual certificate.
assumptions_latex: \(E,F\) are finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces.
\(K\subseteq E\) is a nonempty closed convex cone.
\(A:E\to F\) is linear and \(b\in F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(b\notin\operatorname{cl}A(K)\), equivalently \(\exists y: A^*y\in K^*\) and \(\langle b,y\rangle<0\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strong infeasibility of a primal–dual SDP pair
knowledge_statements.scope_note: For the paired primal and dual semidefinite programs, with a comparison to linear programming.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The primal problem \((P)\) is strongly infeasible if the dual problem \((D)\) has an improving ray; symmetrically, \((D)\) is strongly infeasible if \((P)\) has an improving ray. Every infeasible linear program is strongly infeasible, whereas an infeasible semidefinite program may instead be weakly infeasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A member of a primal–dual SDP pair is strongly infeasible when its opposite problem has an improving ray. All infeasible linear programs satisfy this condition, but semidefinite programs can exhibit weak infeasibility.
assumptions_latex: (P)\text{ and }(D)\text{ form the primal--dual semidefinite-program pair}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (P)\text{ strongly infeasible}\iff(D)\text{ has an improving ray},\qquad (D)\text{ strongly infeasible}\iff(P)\text{ has an improving ray};\qquad \text{infeasible LP}\implies\text{strongly infeasible, but this implication fails for SDP in general}.
knowledge_statements.title: Strong infeasibility of a primal–dual SDP pair
Weakly Infeasible Cone Programs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Image-space definition distinguishing unattained limiting feasibility from strict separation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(K\subseteq E\) be a nonempty closed convex cone, let \(A:E\to F\) be linear, and let \(b\in F\). The system \(Ax=b\), \(x\in K\), is weakly infeasible when
\[
b\in\operatorname{cl}A(K)\setminus A(K).
\]
Equivalently, no feasible \(x\in K\) exists, but
\[
\inf_{x\in K}\|Ax-b\|=0.
\]
Hence arbitrarily small feasibility residuals are attainable although exact feasibility and strict separation both fail.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A weakly infeasible system has no feasible point, yet cone points can attain residuals arbitrarily close to zero.
assumptions_latex: \(E,F\) are finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces.
\(K\subseteq E\) is a nonempty closed convex cone.
\(A:E\to F\) is linear and \(b\in F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(b\in\operatorname{cl}A(K)\setminus A(K)\), equivalently \(\inf_{x\in K}\|Ax-b\|=0\) with no feasible \(x\).

notation.meaning: linear image of K under A

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Weak infeasibility of primal and dual semidefinite programs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes infeasible SDP systems whose respective feasibility residuals can be made arbitrarily small.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The primal problem is weakly infeasible if \(\mathcal P=\varnothing\) and, for every \(\epsilon>0\), there exists \(X\succeq0\) such that \(\lvert\operatorname{Tr}(A_iX)-b_i\rvert\leq\epsilon\) for every \(i\). The dual problem is weakly infeasible if \(\mathcal D=\varnothing\) and, for every \(\epsilon>0\), there exist \(y\in\mathbb R^m\) and \(S\succeq0\) such that \(\left\|\sum_{i=1}^m y_iA_i+S-C\right\|\leq\epsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A primal or dual SDP is weakly infeasible when its feasible set is empty but its corresponding feasibility residual can be made arbitrarily small using positive-semidefinite variables.
assumptions_latex: A_i,C\in\mathbb S^n\quad(i=1,\ldots,m),\qquad b\in\mathbb R^m
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal P=\varnothing\ \land\ \forall\epsilon>0\ \exists X\succeq0:\ \max_i\lvert\operatorname{Tr}(A_iX)-b_i\rvert\leq\epsilon;\qquad \mathcal D=\varnothing\ \land\ \forall\epsilon>0\ \exists y\in\mathbb R^m,\ S\succeq0:\ \left\|\sum_i y_iA_i+S-C\right\|\leq\epsilon.
knowledge_statements.title: Weak infeasibility of primal and dual semidefinite programs
Nonclosed Linear-Image Pathologies
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure mechanism underlying unattained conic feasibility limits.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(K\subseteq E\) be a closed convex cone and \(A:E\to F\) be linear. A nonclosed linear-image pathology occurs when
\[
A(K)\neq\operatorname{cl}A(K).
\]
For every \(b\in\operatorname{cl}A(K)\setminus A(K)\), the system \(Ax=b\), \(x\in K\), is infeasible while
\[
\inf_{x\in K}\|Ax-b\|=0.
\]
Consequently, residual convergence alone cannot distinguish exact feasibility from weak infeasibility at such a boundary point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If a closed cone has a nonclosed linear image, boundary points omitted from that image generate infeasible systems with arbitrarily small residuals.
assumptions_latex: \(E,F\) are finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces.
\(K\subseteq E\) is a closed convex cone.
\(A:E\to F\) is linear.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(b\in\operatorname{cl}A(K)\setminus A(K)\Rightarrow \inf_{x\in K}\|Ax-b\|=0\) without attainment.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: finite-dimensional closure characterization of weak infeasibility

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind fits and the finite-dimensional claim correctly describes how omitted closure points produce weak infeasibility, but no inspectable source is cited for this nonclosed-image pathology.

knowledge_statements.title: Facial-Reduction Dependency
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimal-face reformulation of a feasible system lacking relative strict feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(S=K\cap\{x:Ax=b\}\) be nonempty and suppose \(S\cap\operatorname{ri}K=\varnothing\). Let \(F_{\min}\) be the smallest face of \(K\) containing \(S\). Then \(F_{\min}\) is a proper face and
\[
S=F_{\min}\cap\{x:Ax=b\},
\qquad
S\cap\operatorname{ri}F_{\min}\neq\varnothing.
\]
Thus replacing \(K\) by its minimal feasible face preserves the feasible set and restores relative strict feasibility; diagnostics based on interiority depend on identifying this face.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A weakly feasible system becomes relatively strictly feasible after restricting the cone to the minimal face containing its feasible set.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a closed convex cone in a finite-dimensional Euclidean space.
\(S=K\cap\{x:Ax=b\}\neq\varnothing\).
\(S\cap\operatorname{ri}K=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_{\min}\subsetneq K\), \(S=F_{\min}\cap\{x:Ax=b\}\), and \(S\cap\operatorname{ri}F_{\min}\neq\varnothing\).

notation.meaning: minimal face of K containing the feasible set
